## CHAPTER 4 — CHARACTER: WHO IS ON CAMERA?

### SLIDE 01 — WHO IS ON CAMERA?

\[0:00-1:00\] · On screen: One large question — Who should the audience see and hear? — then, after a beat, beneath it: A persona is constructed. Character already exists. The typography echoes the Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 openings.  
Purpose of this slide: Open the chapter with its controlling question and kill the persona myth at the door (4.1).  
Say:  
"Chapter 2 gave you the framework. We begin at its first letter, with the question that comes before cameras and platforms: who should the audience see and hear?  
Every business already has a character. It may be the owner who has solved the same problems for twenty years. The mistake is assuming every business needs the same kind of person on camera.  
A persona is constructed for public consumption. Character already exists beneath it. We ask what professional character is already there, and how to express it.  
This environment rewards personality, but personality is not performance. The attorney who imitates an energetic influencer does not gain attention — he loses credibility. Not because he cannot perform the style, but because the style does not belong to him."  
Cue: Land "does not belong to him" and stop. This is the sentence that relieves the room.  
---

### SLIDE 02 — AUTHENTIC AUTHORITY

\[1:00-1:55\] · On screen: Two lines held apart: Be yourself above Be effective. Between them, revealed last: Separate skills. Both required.  
Purpose of this slide: Correct the half-truth that authenticity alone is enough, and locate where authority actually lives (4.2).  
Say:  
"Authenticity is usually misunderstood as simply being yourself, and the incompleteness matters.  
A person can be completely authentic and still be ineffective on camera. They can speak too quietly, bury the important point, or use terminology nobody outside their industry understands. Authenticity and effectiveness are separate skills, and they have to work together.  
Authentic authority begins with something real: experience, knowledge, responsibility or results. The camera does not create any of that; it is the channel through which authority becomes visible.  
And for an established business, the assets are already inside. The owner has stories. Salespeople have heard the same objection three hundred times. That is authority, and our job is to extract it."  
---

### SLIDE 03 — THE BUSINESS OWNER AS AUTHORITY

\[1:55-2:51\] · On screen: A sealed container labelled Knowledge, with flow arrows that stop at the wall. Beneath, after the third step: Not the only face. Sometimes the right one.  
Purpose of this slide: Name the most common authority source, and refuse the assumption that it must therefore be permanent (4.3).  
Say:  
"For many small and midsized businesses, the owner is the most obvious source of authority.  
The owner may have started the company and accumulated decades of judgement. Yet that knowledge stays trapped inside conversations with customers who already bought. Nobody else ever hears it.  
A website can describe the company and list its services. It cannot communicate the judgement of the person who built it. Video can: why the company does something differently, what a customer should know before purchasing.  
But notice what I am not saying. The owner may be the best authority source and the wrong person to produce every piece of content. The goal is the right role, not the owner in every frame."  
---

### SLIDE 04 — THE FOUNDER AS THE FACE OF THE COMPANY

\[2:51-3:53\] · On screen: A twelve-week cadence grid that fills with repeatable formats. Beneath: A founder should never wake up wondering what to say.  
Purpose of this slide: Distinguish a founder-led operation from casual content, and hand over the sustainability requirement (4.4).  
Say:  
"Some businesses are inseparable from their founders. The founder's reputation, philosophy and history are a substantial part of the company's identity, and that founder may want to become its recognisable voice.  
Understand what that commitment is: a different order of obligation than occasionally recording a company video. The founder becomes an ongoing media presence, so we have to address not only how they look and sound, but how the presence is sustained.  
A founder-led operation needs repeatable subjects, formats, recording habits and boundaries. The founder should never wake up wondering what to say.  
The raw material is already there: decisions, failures, lessons. The challenge is converting experience into communicable material without turning every video into a corporate announcement. That is a Character problem before it is a production problem."  
---

### SLIDE 05 — THE PROFESSIONAL PRACTITIONER AS AUTHORITY

\[3:53-4:54\] · On screen: A real hierarchy with the highest box greyed out, and an arrow departing toward a lower box. Beneath: The content should follow the authority, not the org chart.  
Purpose of this slide: Detach authority from seniority, and reframe this as organisational depth (4.5).  
Say:  
"Many businesses have a natural authority figure who is not the owner.  
A medical practice has specialists. A law firm has attorneys by area of expertise. A construction company has experienced tradespeople. The question then changes: not who owns this business, but who possesses the knowledge the audience wants.  
The answer may not be the person with the highest title. A practitioner who explains a complicated issue clearly is often more valuable on camera than an executive who merely represents the organisation. The content should follow the authority, not the org chart.  
And there is something better underneath this: the business demonstrates its own depth — a network of knowledgeable voices, instead of one person representing every subject. That is evidence of expertise no competitor can copy."  
---

### SLIDE 06 — THE EMPLOYEE AS SPOKESPERSON

\[4:54-5:51\] · On screen: Two states: "Make some videos" greyed on the left, Prepared spokesperson in accent on the right, with boundaries between them.  
Purpose of this slide: Give permission to use employees, and define what separates a spokesperson from a volunteer (4.6).  
Say:  
"You do not have to put the owner or the founder on camera.  
Some organisations already employ people who communicate naturally — salespeople, customer-service representatives, technicians. They become effective spokespeople when their role, knowledge and style fit what the content is trying to achieve.  
But hold on to one distinction: the employee told to make some videos, against the spokesperson deliberately prepared for the responsibility. The first produces inconsistent content and occasional embarrassment. The second produces a voice the market trusts.  
What separates them is boundaries. A spokesperson needs to know what they can say, what requires approval, and when to redirect a question to somebody else. So we treat spokesperson development as a communication skill and an operational responsibility."  
---

### SLIDE 07 — MULTIPLE SPOKESPEOPLE

\[5:51-6:46\] · On screen: Five department nodes — Marketing · Sales · Operations · Technical · Leadership — each gaining a voice label in sequence.  
Purpose of this slide: Present the distributed model as the mature answer for larger organisations (4.7).  
Say:  
"Larger businesses often have no single person who should carry the entire content operation. That is not a problem to solve. It is an asset to use.  
Different departments hold different forms of authority. Marketing understands the brand. Sales understands the objections. Operations understands delivery.  
One person becomes the primary public voice. Others appear for their subjects — a specialist answers technical questions, a salesperson walks through a real customer scenario.  
That is a distributed authority model, and the operational value is this: the company is no longer dependent on one person having enough time, energy and ideas to produce everything. An operation resting on a single founder has built a bottleneck, probably without noticing."  
---

### SLIDE 08 — PERSONAL BRAND VS. CORPORATE BRAND

\[6:46-7:49\] · On screen: Two overlapping circles labelled Person and Company. A dashed arrow leaves the person, with the question What happens if they leave?  
Purpose of this slide: Surface the dependency risk and licence a range of legitimate models (4.8).  
Say:  
"A personal brand and a corporate brand can overlap, but they are not the same thing.  
A personal brand is centred on an individual the audience follows. A corporate brand belongs to the organisation, not to any one person.  
So ask the question that makes the distinction urgent: what if that person leaves? If every piece of content depends on one founder, you have built an audience relationship and a dependency at the same time. Conversely, refusing to show any human being makes a company unnecessarily impersonal.  
There is no universally correct model. Some businesses build around one person; some use a primary spokesperson supported by specialists; some maintain a corporate identity with many contributors. The right model is the one that supports the business, not the one that looks like somebody else's."  
---

### SLIDE 09 — DEFINING THE ON-CAMERA CHARACTER

\[7:49-8:49\] · On screen: Left, vague adjectives struck through: bold · fun · authentic · energetic. Right, operational questions. Last of them alone: What should they never pretend to know?  
Purpose of this slide: Convert "define your character" from an adjective exercise into an operational specification (4.9).  
Say:  
"The next step is defining how that person should communicate.  
This is usually done badly. It is not a personality document filled with adjectives — bold, fun, authentic, energetic. Those words are too vague to guide a decision: if you cannot tell whether a sentence belongs, the definition is not doing any work.  
A useful definition is operational. How should this person speak? How formal is the language? Which subjects belong naturally to them, and which should be handled by somebody else?  
And one question belongs at the top of the list: what should they never pretend to know? The objective is a recognisable pattern: strong enough that a viewer knows who is speaking without seeing the logo, and flexible enough for a different subject."  
---

### SLIDE 10 — IDENTIFYING EXISTING AUTHORITY

\[8:49-9:46\] · On screen: Four sources stacked — Experience · Knowledge · Results · Perspective — then the closing question alone: What do I know because I have actually done this?  
Purpose of this slide: Give the inventory method, and replace "what should I post?" with the right first question (4.10).  
Say:  
"Before you create a single topic, identify where your authority actually comes from. It has four sources, taken in order.  
Experience first: years in the industry, unusual assignments, problems you solved more than once.  
Knowledge second: what do you know that the average customer does not, and what do you explain more clearly than your competitors?  
Results third: what have you accomplished, and what outcomes can you discuss? Perspective fourth, which people underestimate: experience sees patterns a newcomer cannot, and knows which claims are inflated.  
Those four are the raw material of Character. So never begin by asking what to post, but by the question that produces something useful: what do I know because I have actually done this?"  
---

### SLIDE 11 — EXPERIENCE AS CONTENT

\[9:46-10:44\] · On screen: A line: "That's just obvious." Crossed out and replaced by "That's exactly what they need."  
Purpose of this slide: Break the expertise curse — the belief that hard-won knowledge is too ordinary to say out loud (4.11).  
Say:  
"Experience is one of the most underused forms of business content, and the reason is a quiet trap.  
A person who has worked in an industry for twenty years assumes what they know is ordinary, because it has become ordinary to them. It is not ordinary to the customer. It never was.  
The contractor who identifies a construction problem at a glance has valuable knowledge. The attorney who knows which mistake repeatedly causes clients trouble has valuable knowledge. Both dismiss it as too obvious to mention.  
So reverse the assumption: what has become obvious to you may be exactly what your audience needs explained. Experience also creates stories, and stories are stronger than statements — they contain circumstances, decisions, consequences and lessons."  
---

### SLIDE 12 — KNOWLEDGE AS CONTENT

\[10:44-11:44\] · On screen: Two arrows in opposite directions: Expert → terminology, conclusions against Audience ← what do they need first? Beneath: Same expertise. Different translation.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the translation move, and connect Character to Audience (4.12).  
Say:  
"Knowledge becomes content when it is organised for another person to understand. That is the largest shift most professionals make.  
A subject-matter expert communicates from inside the subject. The audience receives terminology, assumptions and conclusions, without the reasoning that connects them. To the expert, efficient; to everyone else, a wall.  
Effective authority communication moves the other way: the expert steps outside the subject, asks what the audience needs first, and builds from there.  
This is where Character meets Audience. Character identifies the person who holds the knowledge; Audience determines how it must be translated. The same expert may explain the same subject differently to a homeowner, a purchasing manager or a chief executive. The expertise does not change. The communication does — and that is learnable."  
---

### SLIDE 13 — PERSONALITY WITHOUT PERFORMANCE

\[11:44-12:45\] · On screen: A dial labelled Personality with Suppressed at one end, Theatre at the other, and the marker settling on Controlled authenticity.  
Purpose of this slide: Keep personality in the content without licensing performance, and normalise the adjustment (4.13).  
Say:  
"Personality is valuable in content because people connect with people. But personality should not become theatre.  
There is a difference between allowing personality to appear and manufacturing behaviour for attention. We teach the first.  
So a naturally serious person does not need to become loud. A humorous person does not need to suppress humour. An analytical person does not need to pretend to be spontaneous. The goal is controlled authenticity, not a new personality.  
Some adjustment will still be required, and it is worth normalising before anyone experiences it as failure. Someone fascinating in a one-to-one conversation may find their delivery goes flat when they speak to a lens. Someone energetic in a room may read as excessive on video. Those are communication adjustments, not personality replacements."  
---

### SLIDE 14 — CREDIBILITY WITHOUT CORPORATE STIFFNESS

\[12:45-13:45\] · On screen: Two sample sentences. Left: "We deliver synergistic solutions." Right, in accent: "Here's what we do, and why." The left one is partly rewritten into the right as you watch.  
Purpose of this slide: Reframe professionalism so nobody reads this chapter as a request to be casual (4.14).  
Say:  
"Professionalism does not require stiffness. Be careful here, because people often hear something I am not saying.  
For decades, businesses communicated through highly controlled corporate language: polished, approved, stripped of anything human. That approach reduced certain risks, and also produced communication audiences could ignore without effort.  
Modern business content lets you keep the professionalism and drop the stiffness: replacing unnecessary corporate language with clear language, explaining rather than announcing, and answering questions instead of reciting slogans.  
Because credibility does not come from the register you speak in. It comes from what the person knows, what they have actually done, how accurately they communicate and whether they can support what they say. Nobody becomes less professional by speaking naturally. In most cases the opposite is true."  
---

### SLIDE 15 — BUILDING A CONSISTENT ON-CAMERA IDENTITY

\[13:45-14:46\] · On screen: One column headed Standards — language · subject matter · tone · visual presentation · behaviour. Beside it, appearing after the drift test: Delegation becomes possible.  
Purpose of this slide: Show that consistency is an operating asset, not repetition (4.15).  
Say:  
"Consistency does not mean repeating the same thing or the same shot forever. It means the audience knows what to expect from the person.  
The speaker should have recognisable standards for language, subject matter and tone. Those standards make production easier: the creator stops reinventing the identity for every video.  
And they make something else possible as you grow: delegation. If another person helps with scripting, editing or publishing, you can document what the identity should sound and look like. Character becomes part of the operating system, rather than something that lives only inside the creator's head.  
That is the failure mode to guard against. Without documented standards, the communication slowly drifts from the identity that made it work. Nobody decides to change it. It just erodes."  
---

### SLIDE 16 — THE CHARACTER EXERCISE

\[14:46-15:50\] · On screen: One question alone, held for the whole exercise: If your customers could spend thirty minutes with you before deciding whether to hire you, what would they discover?  
Purpose of this slide: Run the discovery exercise, then hand the room over (4.16). This is the Day's first live exercise: 6 minutes of interaction, not speech.  
Say:  
"Now we do the work. Answer this in writing first.  
If your customers could spend thirty minutes with you before deciding whether to hire you, what would they discover that would make them trust your expertise?  
Answer without trying to sound impressive: this is discovery, not promotion. Describe the experiences that shaped your professional judgement, the problems you solve over and over, and the beliefs you hold because of something that actually happened to you.  
Then identify the characteristics that appear naturally when you explain something you genuinely understand. Patient, direct, analytical, warm — none is better than another.  
In a moment I will ask you to record sixty seconds on one subject you know extremely well. No script, no performance. We are not judging the video; we are finding out what is already there."  
Cue: Stop talking here. Take two or three answers from the room before moving on — the six live minutes are spent now.  
---

### SLIDE 17 — THE CHARACTER WORKSHEET

\[15:50-16:55\] · On screen: Six stems revealed in sequence: My professional authority comes from… · People come to me when… · I can explain… · I believe… · I will not pretend to… · When people watch me, I want them to understand that…  
Purpose of this slide: Turn the discovery into a written definition the room can keep (4.17). Completed as homework, not in live time.  
Say:  
"Your worksheet becomes the working definition of your on-camera identity: six sentences, completed as they appear.  
My professional authority comes from — the experiences, knowledge and results that genuinely establish your credibility, not the ones that sound best.  
People come to me when — the problems you are already an authority on. I can explain — the subjects that can become your educational content. I believe — which separates you from generic content, because most competitors never state a position. I will not pretend to — the boundary: authority does not require pretending to know everything.  
And finally: when people watch me, I want them to understand that.  
Then describe the identity in observable behaviour, not adjectives: not professional and engaging, but I explain complicated subjects in plain language — specific enough that somebody else could tell whether a video fits."  
---

### SLIDE 18 — THE CHARACTER IMPLEMENTATION ASSIGNMENT

\[16:55-18:02\] · On screen: Three numbered recordings — 1\. Something they misunderstand · 2\. A story from experience · 3\. An opinion and why you hold it — then four review questions. Completed as homework.  
Purpose of this slide: Hand over the assignment and the review standard (4.18).  
Say:  
"Your assignment turns the definition into behaviour. Three short videos, three different subjects.  
The first explains something your audience frequently misunderstands. The second tells a brief story from your professional experience. The third states a professional opinion, and explains why you hold it. Use the same setup for all three: you are not testing equipment, but Character across three forms of communication.  
Then watch all three and ask four questions instead of judging the production. Does this sound like me? Does it demonstrate something I actually know or have experienced? Would a customer recognise this person as the one they would meet? And what changed when I communicated deliberately rather than just talked?  
What you keep from that review becomes the first version of your On-Camera Character Standard. It will evolve, but it is the foundation for what follows."  
---

### SLIDE 19 — CLOSE OF CHAPTER 4

\[18:02-18:58\] · On screen: Two lines: The camera does not create the authority. Then, alone: It reveals it. Echoes the chapter opening.  
Purpose of this slide: Name Character's place in the framework and hand off to Chapter 5 (chapter close).  
Say:  
"One thing to take from this chapter, because everything else rests on it.  
Character comes first because every other CAMERA dimension depends on knowing who is communicating. Audience decides who they are communicating with. Monetization decides what it has to accomplish. Engagement decides how it earns attention. Repurposing decides how it extends through the business. AI Acceleration decides where tools help without replacing the person whose authority makes the content worth watching.  
So the person who appears on camera must still be the person the customer will meet when the camera is switched off.  
The camera does not create the authority.  
It reveals it.  
Next: how to be that person while a lens is pointed at you."  
Cue: Deliver the last two lines slowly, with a beat between them. It is the chapter's thesis and the handoff to Chapter 5 in the same breath.  
---

## CHAPTER 4 — VISUAL AID SPECIFICATION (TASK 2 — PHASE D INPUT)

Status: nothing here is built. Section 8 puts visuals after the script is approved and after the Step A look gate. This specification exists so the deck can be built against the cut slides rather than the old ones; it is a revision of the earlier Chapter 4 visual aid specification, not a build.  
The standard this chapter is written against. One self-contained HTML file per chapter, 1920 × 1080 stage that scales, no internet, system fonts only. Deep navy-black ground, off-white text, one muted gold accent, quiet steel for secondary text — never more than three colours on a slide. Serif headlines, clean sans elsewhere. Space or right arrow advances one build step, left arrow goes back, every animation ends in a stable final state, and a reduced-motion setting shows the final states with no animation at all.  
The rule added after the round-2 look review: every slide must demonstrate something that changes while the room watches. A labelled diagram is not a demonstration. So each entry below names what actually moves, and the build steps are the number of keypresses.  
New techniques available from the style lock (approved look pending, so these are the intended vocabulary): canvas-filling SVG scenes rather than clip art; material built from gradients only — no glow, no blur, no drop shadow, no neon; a thin specular streak travelling the metal edge instead of an orbiting glow; demonstration by comparison, where two panels run the same process and diverge; and live sorting, drifting or counting rather than static lists.  
Slide 01 — Who Is On Camera. Type: opening question card. Build: 2 steps — the question alone, then the persona/character line beneath. What changes: the second line resolves the question. Why: the controlling question must be legible before any answer appears, and echoing the Chapter 1 and 2 openings signals a new chapter.  
Slide 02 — Authentic Authority. Type: two-lane proof. Build: 3 steps. What changes: a single speaker runs down two lanes at once — the Be yourself lane stays static while the Be effective lane visibly stalls at the same sentences, and the bridge line arrives last showing both are required. Why: the audience's instinct is to treat authenticity and effectiveness as one thing; running them as two lanes that behave differently makes the separation visible instead of asserted.  
Slide 03 — The Business Owner As Authority. Type: sealed-flow diagram. Build: 4 steps. What changes: the owner's knowledge accumulates inside a sealed container — the fill rises — while the outward flow arrows stop dead at the wall; on the final step the wall opens and three channels (why we do it differently, the story behind a service, what to know before buying) begin to move. Why: trapped knowledge is the subsection's argument, and showing the fill rising with nowhere to go is the argument, not an illustration of it.  
Slide 04 — The Founder As The Face. Type: cadence grid. Build: 3 steps. What changes: a twelve-week grid fills cell by cell as repeatable subjects, formats and habits are assigned, then a single cell failure is absorbed without the grid collapsing. Why: the commitment becomes concrete — the sustainability requirement is a filled cadence, not a warning.  
Slide 05 — The Professional Practitioner. Type: corrected hierarchy. Build: 3 steps. What changes: an org chart appears, then the authority marker visibly leaves the highest box and settles on a lower one; the surrounding roles light up in sequence as the network of voices forms. Why: showing authority move away from the top of a hierarchy is instantly understood by owners who already know their best explainer is not their most senior person.  
Slide 06 — The Employee As Spokesperson. Type: two-state contrast. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the same employee node is shown twice; the unprepared version produces output that visibly jitters and diverges, and the prepared version, once the boundary list attaches, produces steady aligned output. Why: it makes the difference between delegation and abandonment a visible property of the output rather than a management claim.  
Slide 07 — Multiple Spokespeople. Type: distributed network with a failure test. Build: 4 steps. What changes: five department nodes each receive a voice in sequence; then one node is removed and the system keeps delivering, whereas a single-founder variant shown beside it stops dead. Why: the no-single-point-of-failure claim is proved by the failure test, not by the diagram.  
Slide 08 — Personal Brand Vs. Corporate Brand. Type: overlap with a departure test. Build: 3 steps. What changes: two circles overlap; the person then leaves, and the audience line visibly snaps back to the company circle, holding at a different (smaller) level. Why: the departure question is what turns an abstract branding distinction into a governance decision, and the visible snap is the decision.  
Slide 09 — Defining The On-Camera Character. Type: admission filter. Build: 3 steps. What changes: three sample sentences are fed past a gate — the vague adjectives are struck as they arrive, and sentences are admitted or rejected against the operational definition, with the never-pretend question left standing alone. Why: an audience that has seen generic brand documents recognises the struck column instantly, and the gate does the arguing without criticising anyone's existing work.  
Slide 10 — Identifying Existing Authority. Type: accumulating inventory. Build: 4 steps. What changes: four sources — experience, knowledge, results, perspective — feed one bar that visibly fills in order, and stops short of full until the final question is asked. Why: this is the chapter's method slide; accumulation is the point, and leaving the bar incomplete makes the closing question operational rather than rhetorical.  
Slide 11 — Experience As Content. Type: before-and-after morph. Build: 2 steps. What changes: "That's just obvious" is struck and replaced by "That's exactly what they need", and three examples of dismissed expertise fade in beneath. Why: the expertise curse is a belief, so the visual has to perform the replacement rather than describe it.  
Slide 12 — Knowledge As Content. Type: re-translation switcher. Build: 3 steps. What changes: one expert statement is held fixed while the audience selector switches between homeowner, purchasing manager and chief executive — the same content re-translates each time, and the expertise line never changes. Why: Character meets Audience on this slide, and the fixed expert line against three moving translations is that meeting made visible.  
Slide 13 — Personality Without Performance. Type: calibrated dial with failure modes. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the dial is driven to each extreme first — suppressed goes flat, theatre spikes — then settles on controlled authenticity, where the trace is recognisable and steady. Why: most first-time presenters fail in one direction or the other, and seeing both extremes fail is more persuasive than being told a midpoint exists.  
Slide 14 — Credibility Without Stiffness. Type: live rewrite. Build: 2 steps. What changes: the corporate sentence "We deliver synergistic solutions" is rewritten in place into "Here's what we do, and why", with the removed words visibly falling away. Why: the room feels the difference instead of being told about it, which prevents the slide being misread as permission to abandon professionalism.  
Slide 15 — A Consistent On-Camera Identity. Type: drift test. Build: 3 steps. What changes: two production tracks run side by side — one with documented standards, one without — and across a run of videos the undocumented track visibly drifts away from the original identity while the documented one holds. Why: the drift warning only lands when the room can watch it happen, and it makes the delegation column a consequence rather than a claim.  
Slide 16 — The Character Exercise. Type: stable prompt. Build: 1 step. What changes: nothing after the reveal — deliberately. Why: the room writes against this slide for six minutes, so it must be stable, legible and free of anything that invites reading instead of thinking.  
Slide 17 — The Character Worksheet. Type: progressive sentence stems. Build: 6 steps, one per stem. What changes: the definition accumulates on screen, each stem staying after its reveal. Why: progressive reveal sets the pace of the homework and lets the presenter take answers between stems.  
Slide 18 — The Implementation Assignment. Type: instruction card with review standard. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the three recordings are numbered in sequence, then the four review questions appear beneath and remain. Why: this is a take-home sheet, and both halves — what to record and how to judge it — must be visible at once so nobody copies it incompletely.  
Slide 19 — Close. Type: statement card echoing Slide 01\. Build: 2 steps — the first line alone, then the final three words. What changes: the thesis resolves to It reveals it. Why: ending in the visual language the chapter opened with tells the room the unit is closed.  
Supplementary — the colleague test (place alongside Slide 15). Type: quick paired exercise. Build: 1 step. What changes: two participants exchange worksheets, and each describes the other's on-camera identity back to them; the gap between intention and impression is the visible result. Why: the only real test of an operational Character definition is whether a second person can apply it, and this produces that evidence in five minutes with no equipment. If it is used in live time it must be counted against the Day's interaction budget, not added on top.

## CHAPTER 5 — ON-CAMERA PRESENCE

### SLIDE 01 — WHY PEOPLE LOOK DIFFERENT ON CAMERA

\[0:00-1:00\] · On screen: One line — The camera adds a layer of awareness. Beneath it, small: Nothing about the person changed.  
Purpose of this slide: Name the universal first-timer experience and reframe the chapter as remaining yourself rather than performing (5.1).  
Say:  
"The camera turns on — and the person talking about their business ten seconds ago becomes someone else. The shoulders tighten, the voice changes, and the eyes drift toward the screen instead of the lens.  
Nothing about that person changed. The camera simply added a layer of awareness. A camera gives you almost none of what a conversation gives you, because a conversation gives you a face and a response. It just watches — which is why awareness turns inward.  
So this chapter is not about becoming more charismatic or more polished. It is about remaining yourself while being observed through a lens. A physician does not need to become an entertainer to communicate the authority they already possess.  
On-camera presence is a learnable professional skill."  
Cue: Land "It just watches." and pause. Everything in this chapter follows from that single difference.  
---

### SLIDE 02 — CAMERA AWARENESS

\[1:00-1:49\] · On screen: Two failure modes side by side — Pretending it isn't there and Conscious of every move — with the centre label: Controlled awareness.  
Purpose of this slide: Separate awareness from anxiety and install the deliberate-choices mindset (5.2).  
Say:  
"Camera awareness is not the same thing as camera anxiety.  
Awareness means understanding that the lens changes how communication is perceived. Distance, framing, lighting and movement all affect what the viewer experiences, and understanding them is what separates deliberate choices from fighting the camera by accident.  
Beginners make one of two mistakes: pretending the camera is not there at all, or becoming so conscious of it that every movement becomes deliberate. Neither produces natural communication.  
The goal is controlled awareness: know where the camera is, where the lens is and what the frame contains, then stop thinking about any of it while you deliver."  
---

### SLIDE 03 — EYE LINE

\[1:49-2:45\] · On screen: A lens with three sight-lines: one direct, two drifting above and beside. Caption: The eye line has to match the situation.  
Purpose of this slide: Establish eye line as the highest-leverage small detail and tie it to the communication situation (5.3).  
Say:  
"Eye line is a small detail with a large effect.  
Look directly into the lens and the viewer experiences eye contact; look slightly above, below or beside it and that relationship changes. Even a small difference reads as distracted, or as though you are speaking to somebody else in the room.  
If the objective is direct communication with the viewer, the lens is the destination. If you are being interviewed, the other person may be the right place to look; demonstrating something on screen, the screen may be correct. No single eye line is universally right; it has to correspond to the communication situation. Get that wrong and the viewer feels a disconnect they cannot name."  
---

### SLIDE 04 — POSTURE AND BODY POSITION

\[2:45-3:50\] · On screen: Split: a collapsed shoulders silhouette beside an over-stiff one, and between them Supported posture. Then a top-down diagram: direct to lens, and three-quarter.  
Purpose of this slide: Replace the posture/posing instinct with a maintainability test, and make body angle a message choice (5.4, 5.5).  
Say:  
"Posture communicates before a word is spoken.  
A collapsed posture makes a knowledgeable person appear uncertain; excessive stiffness creates the opposite problem. Good on-camera posture is not military posture. It is supported posture — arranged so you can breathe naturally, move comfortably and hold a stable relationship with the camera. The head sits over the body rather than being pushed toward the lens, and you can speak for the whole recording without fighting it.  
Body position is the related choice. Facing the lens directly creates one relationship; standing or sitting at an angle creates another. A slight turn adds dimension; an extreme angle makes direct communication harder. Direct instruction wants a straight relationship with the lens; an interview may sit at three-quarter.  
There is no single correct body position — only the one that supports the message."  
---

### SLIDE 05 — FACIAL EXPRESSION

\[3:50-4:39\] · On screen: Three small tiles of the same sentence: serious, warm, bored — captioned Same words. Different meaning.  
Purpose of this slide: Set the standard for the face as honest rather than constant (5.6).  
Say:  
"The camera captures the face in far greater detail than most people expect.  
Small changes in expression change how a statement is interpreted. A neutral expression can read as serious, bored or thoughtful. A smile communicates warmth — until it undermines a serious point.  
The objective is not to manufacture expressions. Artificial expression is easier to recognise on camera than most people believe. Let your face respond to the ideas instead: discussing something exciting, allow the excitement to appear; explaining something complicated, do not feel compelled to hold a permanent smile.  
The camera does not require a constant expression. It requires an honest one."  
---

### SLIDE 06 — HANDS, MOVEMENT AND STILLNESS

\[4:39-5:50\] · On screen: Three panels in sequence: Hands · Movement · Stillness. Under all three, one line: The problem is conscious monitoring.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the body in the frame as one skill — gesture, comfortable setup, and deliberate stillness (5.7, 5.8, 5.9).  
Say:  
"Now the body in the frame — hands, movement and stillness. We take them together because all three break for the same reason: conscious monitoring.  
Some presenters freeze their hands the moment the camera is watching; others start moving them excessively. The useful question is not whether the hands move, but whether the movement belongs to the communication. Gestures carry scale, contrast and importance.  
Natural movement begins with the environment: normal behaviour has to be physically possible. If the chair is uncomfortable you will shift. Some apparent presentation problems are actually production problems.  
And stillness, which is a genuine skill. Many new presenters believe movement creates energy; sometimes it creates visual noise instead. A presenter who can stay still creates a strong sense of attention, and stillness is most powerful on an important statement.  
The goal is control: moving when movement helps, and holding still when stillness communicates more."  
Cue: "Some apparent presentation problems are actually production problems" is the line worth repeating — it is the one that removes blame from the presenter.  
---

### SLIDE 07 — ENERGY

\[5:50-6:46\] · On screen: A volume-style scale labelled Energy, marked with four stops: Quiet authority · Conversational · Urgent · Intense — captioned Energy should serve the subject.  
Purpose of this slide: Replace the "be more energetic" instruction with communicative energy (5.10).  
Say:  
"Energy on camera is frequently misunderstood.  
Presenters are usually told to be more energetic, so they speak louder, move faster and exaggerate their gestures. The result may be technically energetic; it is almost never natural.  
Camera energy is better understood as communicative energy. The camera removes some of the physical presence that exists in a room: a delivery that carries to ten people can land flat on a small screen. So learn the difference between quiet authority, conversational enthusiasm, urgency and intensity. Each has a place, and they do not all belong to the same speaker.  
Energy should serve the subject, reflect the character we defined in Chapter 4, and fit the audience being addressed."  
---

### SLIDE 08 — CONFIDENCE

\[6:46-7:40\] · On screen: A take with one mistake left visible, and beside it: Making mistakes manageable.  
Purpose of this slide: Decouple confidence from perfection and make recovery the skill (5.11).  
Say:  
"Confidence on camera does not mean believing that every sentence will be perfect. Trying to appear perfectly confident usually produces the opposite result.  
Authentic confidence comes from preparation, from knowing the material — and from the ability to recover. A presenter who knows the subject can pause, correct themselves or restart a sentence without losing control of the communication.  
So we separate confidence from perfection. The objective is not to eliminate every mistake, but to make them manageable. A presenter who knows they can stop, breathe and restart is much less likely to tighten up.  
A pause reads as thinking. A rush reads as panic. Audiences forgive the first instantly and remember the second."  
---

### SLIDE 09 — AUTHORITY

\[7:40-8:36\] · On screen: Expertise on one side, viewer on the other, and the space between them labelled: Remove the interference.  
Purpose of this slide: Justify technique as substance, not cosmetics, and reassert that the camera grants nothing (5.12).  
Say:  
"Authority is not created by sounding important. It is created when the viewer has a reason to believe the person speaking understands the subject and can offer useful judgement.  
On-camera presence either strengthens that authority or weakens it. A presenter who speaks clearly, holds an appropriate eye line and controls their pace creates fewer distractions between the viewer and the expertise.  
That is why we do not treat presentation technique as cosmetic. The objective is to remove unnecessary interference between expertise and audience.  
And keep the order right, because this is where businesses go wrong. A business owner does not become an authority because they purchased a better camera. The authority was never the equipment's to give."  
---

### SLIDE 10 — WARMTH

\[8:36-9:28\] · On screen: Two labels held apart: Professional and Impersonal, with an arrow pushing them apart — captioned Do not let the first become the second.  
Purpose of this slide: Set warmth as the guard against impersonality, without prescribing one friendly register (5.13).  
Say:  
"Authority without warmth creates distance — and the right balance depends on the business, the audience and the presenter's own personality.  
Some industries require a highly professional tone; others benefit from informality. Warmth is created through human communication: appropriate expression, conversational language, genuine interest in the audience's problem, and the willingness to speak as a person rather than as a corporate statement.  
We are not trying to make every presenter friendly in exactly the same way. We are preventing professionalism from becoming impersonality.  
A viewer should be able to recognise that there is a real human being behind the expertise. People buy judgement from people they believe they know."  
---

### SLIDE 11 — CONVERSATIONAL PRESENCE

\[9:28-10:29\] · On screen: Two audiences: a stadium on the left, one empty chair on the right. The right one is highlighted.  
Purpose of this slide: Deliver the single most useful mental shift in the chapter (5.14).  
Say:  
"One of the most valuable on-camera skills is speaking to one person rather than to a lens.  
Instead of an invisible audience of thousands, you picture one specific person who needs the information. The words become more direct, the tone more natural, and the explanation easier to follow.  
This is particularly effective in business content, because a business does not have to address the whole market in every video. It can speak to the person who has the problem — so picture sitting across from a client and explaining the issue directly.  
That one shift solves what no technical instruction can. If you are unsure how to say something on camera, ask how you would say it to one person sitting in front of you, and say that."  
---

### SLIDE 12 — AVOIDING "TALKING HEAD" SYNDROME

\[10:29-11:39\] · On screen: One question, large: Does this help the viewer understand, remember, or act? Beneath, smaller: If it does not, it may not belong.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the room a decision rule for production choices, and inoculate against effect-driven editing (5.15).  
Say:  
"A talking-head video is not automatically bad. The problem appears when there is no intentional relationship between the person, the message, the frame and the viewer.  
A static person centred in the frame becomes monotonous when every video uses the same composition, delivery and pacing. The answer is not necessarily more effects; it is better communication design. Framing, movement, demonstrations and supporting visuals can all be used when they genuinely improve the communication.  
Every production choice has to answer one question: does this help the viewer understand, remember, or act? If it does not, it may not belong.  
That discipline matters most once you edit your own content, because modern software makes transitions, zooms and sound effects trivial to add. Accessibility to effects is not a reason for them. Professional content is not defined by how many things move; it is defined by whether the communication works."  
---

### SLIDE 13 — LOOKING INTO THE LENS, AND AT A SCREEN

\[11:39-13:00\] · On screen: One diagram with the lens highlighted and a monitor marked with a warning; caption: Direct-to-camera needs the lens. Conversation needs the person. Demonstration needs the material.  
Purpose of this slide: Handle the two specifics that ruin more takes than anything else in the chapter (5.16, 5.17).  
Say:  
"Two specifics, because these cause more bad footage than anything else in this chapter.  
First, looking into the lens. It feels unnatural at the start: the lens is small and no face looks back. But the viewer experiences the finished image as direct eye contact, so treat the lens as the audience. Practice recordings are how you fix it — record a short statement, watch where your eyes go, then repeat it holding lens contact deliberately. Not staring without blinking.  
Second, looking at a screen, which is not the same thing. Watch yourself on a monitor while recording and you will drift toward your own image, believing you are making eye contact while the viewer sees your eyes looking away.  
That is not always wrong. In a remote interview, the other participant is the natural place to look; demonstrating software, the screen is the subject. The professional skill is knowing which situation you are in: direct-to-camera content requires the lens, conversation requires the person, and demonstration requires the material."  
---

### SLIDE 14 — CAMERA HEIGHT AND DISTANCE

\[13:00-14:13\] · On screen: Three camera positions drawn against the same presenter — low, eye level, high — the eye-level one marked. Then two brackets showing a tight and a wide frame.  
Purpose of this slide: Turn two choices almost nobody makes deliberately into deliberate ones (5.18, 5.19).  
Say:  
"Now the camera itself, and two choices that people almost never make on purpose.  
Height first: a camera below you, at eye level and above you each creates a different impression. Extreme positions can be useful deliberately, but they should never be an accident.  
For most direct-to-camera business communication, the lens should create a natural eye-level relationship. The exact position depends on whether you are standing or sitting. The principle matters more than a number: place the camera deliberately — a phone flat on a desk produces a completely different perspective from the same phone mounted at eye level.  
Distance determines more than how large you appear. It changes perspective, background visibility, how much you can move and the character of the shot. A tight frame creates intensity; a wider frame gives context and room to move. So match the distance to the purpose rather than backing up until your whole body fits."  
---

### SLIDE 15 — FRAMING AND HEADROOM

\[14:13-15:21\] · On screen: One question alone — What is this frame communicating? — then the same shot shown twice, with the headroom indicator under the second: Too much. Too little. Deliberate.  
Purpose of this slide: Move framing from "is my face visible?" to intentional composition, and settle headroom as consistency rather than a rule (5.20, 5.21).  
Say:  
"Framing is the deliberate organisation of everything the viewer sees.  
A good business video is not good merely because a face is visible. So the first question is not whether your face fits. It is: what is this frame communicating? A clean frame can create authority and excessive clutter competes with the presenter.  
Headroom is the specific version of that — the space between the top of your head and the top of the frame. Too much and you look disconnected from the frame; too little and the composition feels cramped or accidental.  
There is no universal number; the right amount depends on the aspect ratio, the distance and the platform. What matters is consistency and intention. Learn to recognise when a composition feels balanced rather than trusting automatic framing — the guides on modern phones should assist your judgement, not replace it."  
---

### SLIDE 16 — BACKGROUND RELATIONSHIP

\[15:21-16:28\] · On screen: Six small environment tiles — office · workshop · treatment room · showroom · kitchen · outdoor — with one test beneath: Does it support the credibility and character we established?  
Purpose of this slide: Make the background a chosen part of the presentation, without prescribing equipment (5.22).  
Say:  
"The presenter does not exist independently of the background.  
The background carries information about the person, the business and the visual identity. It can support the message or compete with it, so treat it as part of the presentation rather than whatever is behind the chair.  
That does not mean every business needs a studio. A clean wall, an office or a workshop can all work — when they are deliberately chosen and properly composed.  
The test is whether the environment supports the credibility and character we established earlier. A lawyer may choose a setting that communicates professionalism; a builder may show where the work actually occurs.  
The background should tell the truth about the business while remaining subordinate to the communication. And depth helps: separating you from the background gives the image dimension, and that comes from positioning rather than equipment."  
---

### SLIDE 17 — THE ON-CAMERA PRESENCE EXERCISE

\[16:28-18:15\] · On screen: Three numbered viewings — 1\. Behaviour · 2\. Sound off · 3\. Image off — and beneath: Pick the two issues that interfere most. Re-record. Compare.  
Purpose of this slide: Run the three-pass review, then hand the room over (5.23). This is the Day's largest live exercise: 8 minutes of interaction, not speech.  
Say:  
"Now we practise, and the exercise is deliberately simple.  
Record sixty seconds explaining something you know extremely well. No script. Do not buy anything. Do not try to make the recording impressive. Use the device you already own, put it in a reasonably comfortable position, and explain one thing to one person.  
Then watch it back without judging whether you look good. Watch first for behaviour. Where did your eyes go? Did you find the lens? Did your posture change? Did your hands stop moving, or start moving too much? Did your voice change? Did you rush? Did your expression match what you were saying?  
Then watch it a second time with the sound off, and evaluate the visual communication alone. Does the person on screen look engaged? Is the body position comfortable? Does the framing look intentional? Is the background distracting?  
Then a third time with the image hidden, listening only to the voice. Does this sound like the person who normally explains this subject? Is the pace natural? Are there filler words? Does the voice become higher, faster or more formal than in conversation?  
That gives you your baseline: what is actually there before we change anything. Do not try to fix everything at once. Choose the two issues that most interfere with communication, record again, and compare the two versions."  
Cue: Stop talking and let them record. The eight live minutes are spent here, and the three viewings take longer than the explanation does.  
---

### SLIDE 18 — SELF-ASSESSMENT

\[18:15-19:34\] · On screen: Three questions revealed in sequence: When the camera turns on, what changes about me? · What do I want the viewer to experience? · What is the smallest change that would improve this immediately?  
Purpose of this slide: Make the participant self-diagnosing rather than dependent on outside judgement, and set the recurring habit (5.24). Completed as homework, not in live time.  
Say:  
"Before we move on, you should be able to describe your own on-camera behaviour without relying on somebody else's judgement. Do this properly this evening, against the recording you just made.  
Start with the question that matters: when the camera turns on, what changes about me? Do I become more formal? Quieter? Do I speak faster? Smile unnecessarily? Do I stop moving, or move too much? Do I look at myself instead of the lens?  
Then a more important question: what do I want the viewer to experience when I communicate? Confidence, trust, expertise, warmth or calm — there is no universal answer, but the desired experience should correspond to the character you defined in Chapter 4\.  
And finally: what is the smallest change I could make that would improve the communication immediately?  
I want that last question to become a habit through the rest of this programme. The goal is a presenter who gradually stops noticing the mechanics, because they have become familiar."  
---

### SLIDE 19 — CLOSE OF CHAPTER 5

\[19:34-20:45\] · On screen: Two lines: The camera stops being an obstacle. Then, alone: It becomes a tool.  
Purpose of this slide: Gather the chapter into one idea and hand off to Chapter 6 (chapter close).  
Say:  
"Let me gather the whole chapter into one idea.  
Everything we covered today — awareness, eye line, posture, movement, energy, authority, warmth, the frame, the background — is not about performing for a lens. It is about removing what stands between your expertise and the person watching.  
Picture two presenters side by side. One is fighting the camera — looking at the wrong place, locked into a stiff position. The other made the technical decisions deliberately and has stopped thinking about them. The viewer cannot see the difference in skill; they can only feel the difference in trust.  
With enough practice, the camera stops being an obstacle.  
It becomes a tool.  
And once you can communicate naturally through that tool, every technical decision that follows — camera, microphone, lighting — can be selected for a reason rather than purchased in search of confidence.  
Next: who is actually on the other side of that lens."  
Cue: Deliver the last line slowly. It is the chapter's thesis and the handoff to Chapter 6 in one breath.  
---

## CHAPTER 5 — VISUAL AID SPECIFICATION (TASK 2 — PHASE D INPUT)

Status: nothing here is built. Section 8 puts visuals after the script is approved and after the Step A look gate. This is a revision of the earlier Chapter 5 visual aid specification, written against the cut slides: the old specification described the same nineteen slides but was written before the cut, so several of its builds no longer match what the presenter says — the energy scale, the environment tile set, the confidence take and the framing examples have each been rebuilt below against the trimmed script. Day 1's other files — Chapters 1, 2 and 4 — carry this same section in this same shape, against the same standard and the same vocabulary.  
The standard this chapter is written against. One self-contained HTML file per chapter, 1920 × 1080 stage that scales, no internet, system fonts only. Deep navy-black ground, off-white text, one muted gold accent, quiet steel for secondary text — never more than three colours on a slide. Serif headlines, clean sans elsewhere. Space or right arrow advances one build step, left arrow goes back, every animation ends in a stable final state, and a reduced-motion setting shows the final states with no animation at all. Body text at least 44 px, captions at least 32 px, lines at least 3 px, an 8% safe margin on all edges, CAMERA wordmark and slide number in the footer, and every chapter-close echoing its chapter's opening typography.  
The rule added after the round-2 look review: every slide must demonstrate something that changes while the room watches. A labelled diagram is not a demonstration — and this is the chapter where that rule bites hardest, because presence is taught through body positions and camera placements that are easy to draw and useless when merely drawn. So each entry below names what actually moves, and the build steps are the number of keypresses.  
New techniques available from the style lock (approved look pending, so these are intended vocabulary, not a claim): canvas-filling SVG scenes rather than clip art; material built from gradients only — no glow, no blur, no drop shadow, no neon; a thin specular streak travelling the metal edge instead of an orbiting glow; demonstration by comparison, where two panels run the same process and diverge; live sorting, drifting or counting rather than static lists; and material held deliberately still where the claim being made is stability. This chapter adds one of its own, because the subject demands it: a body or a camera that is moved on screen, so the room watches a position change rather than reading about it. The few small figures this chapter needs carry the on-screen Illustrative label, and every one of them is a readout on an existing element rather than a chart of its own.  
Slide 01 — Why People Look Different On Camera. Type: layer-insertion demonstration. Build: 2 steps. What changes: a light awareness layer slides in between the presenter and the lens, and three live meters behind the glass — pace, eye line, gesture — drift off their baseline as it arrives, while a caption reading what changed? stays empty; on the second step the caption resolves to Nothing about the person, and the meters hold their new offset rather than snapping back. Why: the chapter's premise is that only awareness changed, and a drift the room can watch — with the person's own figures visibly unchanged underneath — states that better than the sentence does. It also echoes the Chapter 1, 2 and 4 openings, which is how the room knows a new chapter has begun.  
Slide 02 — Camera Awareness. Type: two-extreme instrument with a working centre. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the first extreme runs — the presenter pretends the lens is not there, and the frame drifts until the head leaves the safe area; the second runs — every movement is deliberate, and the trace stutters; the third sets the variables once (distance, framing, lens height) and then greys them out, and the delivery runs clean with nothing left to adjust. Why: both mistakes are recognisable to an executive audience, and the greyed-out panel is the lesson — the choices are made before the take, not during it.  
Slide 03 — Eye Line. Type: sight-line geometry test. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the lens is marked and the direct sight-line drawn; two drifting lines are then drawn above and beside it, and a viewer-side marker shows where each lands — on the viewer's eyes for the direct line, off to one side for the others; the third step adds the three situations, so the same line is shown to be correct in one and wrong in another. Why: a few centimetres of eye travel becomes a large perceptual difference, and landing the marker on or off the viewer's own eyes is that difference made visible. Adding the situations keeps the slide from reading as a rule to memorise.  
Slide 04 — Posture And Body Position. Type: posture-sustain timer plus angle selector. Build: 3 steps. What changes: three postures are held against a running clock — collapsed, over-stiff and supported — and across the run the first two visibly decay, the collapsed one folding further and the stiff one stiffening, while the supported one holds to the end; the third step switches to a top-down view and rotates the same presenter through straight, three-quarter and extreme, marking the relationship each creates with the lens. Why: the maintainability test is the whole argument of §5.4, and decay over time is the only honest way to show it — a still silhouette proves nothing about ten minutes. The angle selector then shows that the body's direction is a message choice rather than a preference.  
Slide 05 — Facial Expression. Type: one sentence, three readings, with a viewer-side readout. Build: 2 steps. What changes: the identical sentence appears with three expression tiles; the first step plays each tile with a readout naming what the viewer receives — serious · warm · bored — while the words never change; the second step holds the honest expression and the readout settles on the meaning the speaker intended. Why: the slide's claim is that the words do not carry the meaning on their own, so the words must be visibly identical while the received meaning changes. A triptych with no readout would show three faces and prove nothing.  
Slide 06 — Hands, Movement And Stillness. Type: movement trace with three panels and one shared cause. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the frozen panel first — the trace is flat and a key word passes with no emphasis; then the excessive panel — the trace is noisy and the same key word is buried in gesture; then the controlled panel — the trace peaks only on the words that carry the point; the shared cause line arrives last, once all three traces are on screen. Why: the three symptoms share one cause, and the cause only becomes persuasive after the room has watched all three traces behave differently. The third panel is also the slide's definition of control, which a still image cannot supply.  
Slide 07 — Energy. Type: register scale matched to a subject. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the scale appears with its four stops — Quiet authority · Conversational · Urgent · Intense — and a fit indicator is empty; a subject then loads into the slide, a serious clinical explanation, and the same sentence is delivered at each stop, with the indicator accepting one register and rejecting three; the third step loads a different subject and the fit moves, while the others stay rejected. Why: the correction being made is the reflex instruction to be more energetic, and a scale that accepts different registers for different subjects shows that energy is matched, not raised. The delivery figures are illustrative and labelled.  
Slide 08 — Confidence. Type: recovery take with the mistake left in. Build: 2 steps. What changes: a take plays with its stumble visible in the trace; on the second step the presenter pauses, breathes and restarts, and a calm meter that dropped at the stumble recovers and ends above where it started, while the take continues rather than resetting. Why: leaving the mistake in is the argument — a clean take would contradict the slide — and a meter that recovers past its own starting point is what "mistakes manageable" means in practice.  
Slide 09 — Authority. Type: interference-removal channel. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the expertise block and the viewer are placed at either end of a channel; three barriers then arrive inside it as noise — looking away, rushing, reading mechanically — and the signal at the viewer visibly degrades; on the third step each barrier is removed in turn and the signal clears, with the expertise block's own value reading unchanged throughout. Why: the slide argues that technique removes interference rather than adding authority, and an unchanged expertise figure beside a cleared signal is that argument as a measurement. It is also the antidote to an audience that reads this chapter as presentational polish.  
Slide 10 — Warmth. Type: divergence with a keep-out band. Build: 2 steps. What changes: Professional and Impersonal start together; an arrow then pushes them apart, and as the drift proceeds the marker of the recognisably human element — expression, conversational language, interest — thins until it is nearly gone, at which point a band labelled the line we do not cross appears between them and the drift stops. Why: the risk being managed is drift from one word into the other, and an arrow shows drift better than a sentence; the band is what keeps the slide from being heard as an instruction to be informal.  
Slide 11 — Conversational Presence. Type: audience-scale switch on one delivery. Build: 2 steps. What changes: the stadium runs first — thousands of targets, and the delivery measurably degrades, pace up and fillers up, with the messaging readout vague; the switch to the single chair re-runs the same content and the figures settle, with the readout becoming specific. Why: this is the chapter's most transferable technique, and the switch makes the mechanism visible: the only thing that changed is who the speaker imagined. The two sets of figures are illustrative and labelled.  
Slide 12 — Avoiding "Talking Head" Syndrome. Type: decision gate on production choices. Build: 3 steps. What changes: candidate choices are fed past the one question — a transition, a zoom, a cutaway, a screen recording, a caption — and each is admitted or rejected on what it does for understanding, memory or action; admitted choices visibly improve the frame while the rejected pile stacks; the third step holds the question alone. Why: a gate that rejects some furniture is what stops the chapter being heard as an argument against production value, and the closing line about professional content needs the rejected pile still on screen for it to land.  
Slide 13 — Looking Into The Lens, And At A Screen. Type: contact-point map with a warning state. Build: 3 steps. What changes: first the lens is marked, the sight-line lands and the viewer-side contact indicator lights; then the screen and self-view are marked, the line drifts to the presenter's own image, and the indicator shows the contact lost — drawn from the viewer's side, so the room sees what the viewer sees; the third step routes the three situations — direct-to-camera to the lens, conversation to the person, demonstration to the material — and each route lights its own correct contact point. Why: more takes are ruined here than anywhere else in the chapter, and the failure is invisible to the presenter by definition, because they believe they are making eye contact. Showing the loss from the viewer's side is the only version of the slide that can correct that belief.  
Slide 14 — Camera Height And Distance. Type: camera position bench with a distance bracket. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the lens is drawn at three heights against the same presenter — low, eye level, high — and the perspective on the presenter changes as it moves, with eye level marked; the accident case follows, the laptop set wherever it fit, and the frame shows what that costs; the third step slides the bracket from tight to wide, and the frame's contents change — intensity against context and room to move. Why: both sections are about choices nobody makes on purpose, so the bench has to show the accident and the decision side by side. Moving the bracket rather than swapping two still images shows that distance governs what is in the frame, not only how large the presenter looks.  
Slide 15 — Framing And Headroom. Type: frame audit on one composition. Build: 3 steps. What changes: one shot is held while a readout answers the slide's question for each version — headroom too generous returns disconnected; headroom too tight returns cramped; the deliberate version returns the composition's actual message, and a piece of clutter is then removed from the frame and the readout sharpens. Why: the slide moves the question from whether a face fits to what the frame communicates, and a readout that answers differently for each version is that move made mechanical. The cue invites asking the room what the frame says, so the readout is the last thing to appear.  
Slide 16 — Background Relationship. Type: environment selection with a depth test. Build: 3 steps. What changes: the environment tiles appear and the presenter is placed into three of them in turn, each with a supporting-or-competing verdict shown beside it; the third step makes a single depth move — the presenter steps forward from the background — and the image visibly gains dimension with no equipment added. Why: the section's test is whether the environment supports the credibility already established, and a verdict against each placement is that test applied rather than described. The depth move is the slide's proof that this is positioning, not purchasing, which is the anti-equipment claim running through the chapter.  
Slide 17 — The On-Camera Presence Exercise. Type: stable prompt across three passes. Build: 3 steps, one per viewing pass. What changes: only the active pass mark advances — 1\. Behaviour · 2\. Sound off · 3\. Image off — and each pass lights its own line of what to watch; after the third, the closing instruction, pick the two issues that interfere most, re-record, compare, holds for the rest of the exercise. Why: the room records and reviews against this slide for eight minutes, so it has to remain stable and legible at a distance, and the three passes must never be conflated — the whole exercise depends on separating what the eyes did from what the voice did.  
Slide 18 — Self-Assessment. Type: progressive questions with a smallest-change lock. Build: 3 steps, one per question. What changes: each question arrives and stays, so the sequence accumulates; the third — what is the smallest change that would improve this immediately? — locks in accent and holds after the first two drop to steel. Why: this is the recurring habit the chapter installs, and it only lands after the participant has answered the first two about themselves. Completing it as homework is deliberate: it is answered against the recording they made, which is why it is not live time.  
Slide 19 — Close Of Chapter 5\. Type: statement card echoing Slide 01, with the interference clearing. Build: 2 steps. What changes: the two lines arrive in order and the awareness layer from Slide 01 is lifted away as the second one lands; then the paired-presenter comparison the presenter described draws itself once — one fighting the camera, one no longer noticing it — and holds. Why: closing in the opening's visual language signals the unit is closed, and lifting the layer is the chapter's whole argument performed rather than restated. The paired comparison is the hand-off: the difference the room should feel is trust, not skill.  
Supplementary — the thirty-second eye-line drill (place alongside Slide 13). Type: quick paired exercise. Build: 1 step. What changes: each participant records a thirty-second statement twice — once speaking naturally, once holding the lens deliberately — and the two takes play side by side with the contact-point indicator from Slide 13 above each. Why: eye line is the highest-leverage correction in the chapter and the one most quickly felt rather than explained, and two takes recorded back-to-back produce the evidence in about five minutes with no equipment beyond the phone already in the room. Chapter 5's live exercise time is already fully spent on the eight minutes of Slide 17, so if this drill is used in live time it is charged against the Day's interaction budget and traded out of another chapter rather than added on top; it also works as homework alongside the Self-Assessment.
