## CHAPTER 10 — UNDERSTANDING ATTENTION

### SLIDE 01 — THE ECONOMICS OF ATTENTION

\[0:00-0:55\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 01 / 13\. Claim, serif: Attention is a finite budget, and every minute of your content is a bid against everything else on the screen. Structure: a gate / flow — left labelled the broadcast room: a handful of alternatives in that moment, right labelled the feed: an unlimited number, one thumb-flick away; the same thirty-second window drawn across both, with one exit under each. Evidence: a cost ledger running the same thirty seconds twice — alternatives available in the room against alternatives available on the phone in front of them — marked Illustrative, provenance line Illustrative — a demonstration, not a measured figure. Consequence, accent: You are not competing with your industry. You are competing with everything else on the screen.  
Purpose of this slide: Put the chapter's mechanism in place before any technique is taught, and open the Engagement block (10.1).  
Say:  
"Everything in this programme assumes one thing: that the content gets watched. Nothing we have built so far matters if the viewer scrolls past before any of it has a chance.  
Attention behaves like a limited resource, because it is one. Each person has a finite amount of time and mental bandwidth, and an effectively unlimited supply of content bidding for it.  
That is a different environment from the one marketing was invented in. A viewer in a commercial break had a handful of alternatives; a viewer in a feed has an unlimited number, a thumb-flick away.  
Accurate and useful is not enough: content has to earn the attention required for anyone to discover it."  
Cue: Land the two columns and stop. The chapter does not argue that attention matters; it assumes the room already knows, and spends its time on the mechanism.  
---

### SLIDE 02 — WHY PEOPLE STOP SCROLLING

\[0:55-1:49\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 02 / 13\. Claim, serif: Nobody reads your content's contents page. They judge it in a fraction of a second. Structure: a scorecard — three labelled rows the viewer's mind answers instantly: does this apply to me · does this matter · is there a reason to keep watching, each marked as answered or unanswered. Evidence: the same three rows re-scored for a genuine piece that was never watched, provenance line From CAMERA Ch. 10 §10.2. Consequence, accent: A great piece that nobody pauses for is indistinguishable, in business terms, from one that was never made.  
Purpose of this slide: Define what the instantaneous judgement is actually evaluating, and why value alone does not earn attention (10.2).  
Say:  
"People do not evaluate content by reading a description first. They make an almost instantaneous judgement, often without being aware of making one, from very little: an image, a few words, a tone, a face.  
In practice it answers three questions. Does this apply to me? Does this matter? Is there a reason to keep watching?  
Content can fail to earn attention not because it lacks value but because it never communicates that value fast enough to register. A business can make something excellent that nobody watches, because the opening gave no reason to pause.  
Engagement is not a separate concern from substance: the opening decides whether the substance is ever experienced."  
Cue: The three questions are the chapter's spine — the next five slides are the tools that answer them. Say so, then move.  
---

### SLIDE 03 — THE FIRST FRAME

\[1:49-2:42\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 03 / 13\. Claim, serif: Before you say a word, the first frame has already made your case — or lost it. Structure: a comparison ledger — two first frames side by side, matched on every row that matters: who is speaking · what environment is this · what is about to happen, each row marked legible or unreadable. Evidence: a one-second read test on each frame, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 10 §10.3. Consequence, accent: Compose the first frame deliberately. It is doing the selling before you open your mouth.  
Purpose of this slide: Make the opening image a deliberate decision rather than a by-product of turning the camera on (10.3).  
Say:  
"Before a single word is spoken, the first frame is already communicating.  
A cluttered or confusing frame loses viewers before any explanation clarifies what they are looking at. A clear frame that says who is speaking, where they are and what is happening buys time for the opening words.  
This does not mean elaborate production. It means being deliberate about what the first image communicates. A presenter looking clearly into the lens, in a frame that makes sense, routinely beats a more elaborate opening that takes time to become legible.  
The first frame answers a question the viewer has not asked: what is this, and is it worth my attention?"  
Cue: Point out that this is a decision they can make in ten seconds before every recording, which is what makes it worth teaching.  
---

### SLIDE 04 — THE FIRST SENTENCE

\[2:42-3:36\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 04 / 13\. Claim, serif: Your first sentence is not an introduction. It is the reason someone decides to keep listening. Structure: a cost ledger — the same opening second spent two ways: a preamble (hi, I'm … and today I want to talk about …) against a relevant statement, with the audience still present after each. Evidence: the preamble written out in full and struck through as the room watches it fail, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 10 §10.4. Consequence, accent: Put your credentials after the reason to listen, never in front of it.  
Purpose of this slide: Move the introduction out of the opening and the relevance into it (10.4).  
Say:  
"If the frame earns a moment of visual attention, the first sentence earns the decision to keep listening.  
The first sentence should not be a preamble, an introduction of the speaker, or a list of what the video covers. It should signal relevance immediately — a problem, a question, or a statement that gives the viewer a reason to stay.  
The classic mistake is opening with: hi, I'm so-and-so, and today I want to talk about a broad topic. That delays the actual reason to pay attention until after the audience has had every chance to leave.  
A stronger opening states the relevant thing first; introductions follow once they have decided to stay."  
Cue: Most rooms in this programme open with the preamble. Say plainly that it is the single easiest fix in the chapter.  
---

### SLIDE 05 — THE FIRST THREE SECONDS

\[3:36-4:32\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 05 / 13\. Claim, serif: Three seconds decide whether the next three minutes exist for anyone but you. Structure: a timeline with milestones — one three-second window divided into what the viewer is evaluating at once: the frame · the first words · the tone · whether this fits me, with the segment spent on introductions marked as spent. Evidence: the same opening reviewed twice, with the second listing what those three seconds now do, provenance line From your own published content. Consequence, accent: Ask what happens in your first three seconds. If the honest answer is nothing, rebuild the opening before you touch anything else.  
Purpose of this slide: Concentrate the preceding two slides into the window that actually decides it, and hand the room a review habit (10.5).  
Say:  
"The first three seconds often determine whether anything that follows will ever be seen.  
That is not a marketing statistic; it reflects how fast that judgement runs when there are unlimited alternatives. In those seconds the viewer weighs the frame, the first words, the tone and an impression of fit. Spend them on introductions or a slow visual setup and your most valuable seconds are gone.  
This does not mean frantic or shocking, only that the opening is built knowing most of the decision happens immediately.  
So review a finished piece and ask: what happens in my first three seconds, and would a stranger keep watching? If the answer is no, fix the opening before anything else."  
Cue: This is the check the room will actually run. Give them the question verbatim and let them write it down.  
---

### SLIDE 06 — RELEVANCE

\[4:32-5:29\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 06 / 13\. Claim, serif: Broadly related to your industry is not relevance. It is the reason nobody recognises themselves in your opening. Structure: a 2 × 2 matrix — axes general ↔ specific relevance against explicitly stated ↔ implicitly signalled — with four sample openings placed in their quadrants and the specific-explicit quadrant left lit as the one that pulls. Evidence: two openings placed side by side, the first addressed to an industry and the second to a situation the viewer is in today, provenance line From your Chapter 6 audience profile. Consequence, accent: Write the opening to one person's Tuesday, not to a market.  
Purpose of this slide: Split general from specific relevance, and connect the opening back to the Audience work (10.6).  
Say:  
"Relevance is the single most important factor in whether someone keeps watching, and it is more specific than being related to your field.  
Content is relevant when the viewer immediately recognises it applies to their situation, question or problem. General relevance — broadly related to an industry — is far weaker than specific relevance, which speaks to something they are experiencing today.  
This is where the Audience work decides how effective an opening can be. Know your audience's specific problems and you can build an opening that speaks to them. Without that, you produce openings related to your field and relevant to nobody.  
Relevance can be stated or signalled; either way, they should recognise within moments that this applies to them."  
Cue: Push back on anyone who wants to sound like the whole industry. Relevance is a target, not a tone.  
---

### SLIDE 07 — CURIOSITY

\[5:29-6:24\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 07 / 13\. Claim, serif: Curiosity is a gap between what they know and what they want to know — and you have to be willing to fill it. Structure: a quote panel — one honest gap stated in a single line and deliberately left open, with the closing rule beneath: the content must close it. Evidence: the same gap restated as a manufactured one, where the promise is bigger than the payload, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 10 §10.7. Consequence, accent: Open a gap you intend to close. Anything else is borrowing trust you will have to pay back.  
Purpose of this slide: Establish curiosity as an honest tool rather than a withheld answer (10.7).  
Say:  
"Curiosity holds attention by creating a gap between what the viewer knows and what they want to know.  
Raise a genuine question and hold the answer, and attention sustains itself: they keep watching to close the gap. That might be an unexpected statement, an incomplete explanation, or a question you promise to answer.  
Used carelessly it becomes clickbait, which is this chapter's last slide. Genuine curiosity closes a gap the viewer already cares about. Manufactured curiosity withholds something they never cared about, or implies something the content does not deliver — and the moment they notice, trust goes.  
Used honestly it is the strongest tool here, because it works with their attention rather than against it."  
Cue: Keep the distinction concrete: the test is not how big the gap is, but whether the content closes it.  
---

### SLIDE 08 — TENSION

\[6:24-7:21\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 08 / 13\. Claim, serif: Tension is not drama. It is an unresolved problem the viewer wants to see settled. Structure: a ladder / stack — a real situation rising through what could go wrong · what it costs · what was decided · how it ended, with the outcome held off until the top rung. Evidence: a customer situation resolved the wrong way round — solution first — and the same situation built from the problem up, provenance line From your own case history. Consequence, accent: Show the problem before the solution, or you will be teaching a fix to people who do not yet know they need it.  
Purpose of this slide: Separate tension from curiosity and from manufactured drama (10.8).  
Say:  
"Tension is an unresolved problem, conflict or uncertainty that the viewer wants to see settled.  
That differs from curiosity, which is about missing information. Tension is about stakes: something that could go wrong, a decision with consequences. A customer who nearly made an expensive mistake holds attention because the outcome is uncertain.  
It is built through storytelling, through how a problem is framed, or through an explanation that builds toward a resolution rather than announcing it. A demonstration that makes the problem clear before the solution uses tension; one that explains the solution first wastes it.  
Business content does not need invented drama. Real situations carry enough tension already — the work is structuring the content to reveal it."  
Cue: Say the last sentence slowly. Owners assume tension means theatre; here it means order.  
---

### SLIDE 09 — SPECIFICITY

\[7:21-8:15\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 09 / 13\. Claim, serif: Specificity is the cheapest proof of experience you own, and generalities give it away for nothing. Structure: an evidence wall — four pairs of matched phrases landing one at a time, each pair showing the general version beside the specific one: numbers · situations · timeframes · language. Evidence: two phrasings side by side — many people struggle with this against the mistake we see in about half the properties we inspect — with the second marked as the one that could only have come from the business, provenance line From your own records, or labelled Illustrative if the count is not verified. Consequence, accent: Replace the general claim with the count, the timeframe or the situation you actually saw.  
Purpose of this slide: Make specificity a mechanical habit, and tie it back to information versus insight (10.9).  
Say:  
"Specific content holds attention better than general content, because specificity signals real and particular knowledge rather than an understanding anyone could have.  
Many people struggle with this is general and easy to dismiss. The mistake we see in half the properties we inspect earns attention and trust, because it sounds like direct experience.  
Specificity applies to numbers, situations, timeframes and language. Vague phrasing invites a vague response: mild interest at best. Concrete phrasing invites real attention, because it tells the viewer that what comes next will be equally concrete.  
This is the distinction we drew between information and insight: specific content demonstrates the judgement that separates you from everyone saying something similar."  
Cue: Warn them about invented precision here: specific means true and checkable, not rounded up for effect. That is where the label on the slide comes from.  
---

### SLIDE 10 — STAKES

\[8:15-9:06\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 10 / 13\. Claim, serif: Consequence is what makes information worth attending to; without it, you are just describing things. Structure: a decision bench — the same problem stated twice, once in abstract terms and once with what it costs, judged against rows: time · money · safety · outcome, with inflated stakes shown losing the same rows. Evidence: the business's own most common problem written with its real consequence and with an exaggeration beside it, provenance line From your own service history. Consequence, accent: Name what the mistake costs. Then stop — do not inflate it.  
Purpose of this slide: Add consequence to attention, and draw the line at exaggeration (10.10).  
Say:  
"Stakes are what the viewer stands to gain or lose depending on whether they understand and act on what you are saying.  
Content that establishes stakes — even modest ones — holds attention better than information with no sense of consequence. Someone keeps watching an explanation of a mistake if they know what it costs, in time, money, safety or outcome.  
Establishing stakes does not require exaggeration. Most business problems already carry genuine consequences: wasted money, lost time, safety, missed opportunity. Making those clear and specific is usually enough.  
Resist inflating them. Exaggerated stakes are recognised as manipulation, and that damages exactly the trust engagement is meant to build."  
Cue: This slide is the ethical boundary of the chapter. Say that the room's own credibility is the thing being protected.  
---

### SLIDE 11 — PATTERN INTERRUPTS

\[9:06-10:06\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 11 / 13\. Claim, serif: Viewers have learned to scroll past you; the only way past that is to be visibly not the pattern. Structure: a timeline with milestones — a familiar pattern scrolling by untouched, an interrupt landing, and the pattern resuming — with the interrupt marked as either connected to the substance or connected to nothing. Evidence: two interrupts matched against the content that follows, one that the content honours and one that it does not, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 10 §10.11. Consequence, accent: Interrupt with something the content actually delivers, or you have taught them to distrust your openings.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the room the interrupt, and its condition of use (10.11).  
Say:  
"A pattern interrupt breaks the viewer's expectation of what is about to happen, and captures attention because it is not what they have learned to scroll past.  
Viewers have an almost unconscious sense of what typical content looks like, and much of it is easy to ignore. Something that visibly departs from it — an unexpected visual, an unusual statement — can interrupt the automatic scroll long enough to register.  
Used carelessly it reads as a trick, and a trick costs trust the moment they notice.  
The ones that work are genuinely connected to the substance: an unexpected fact that turns out to be true and relevant, an unusual demonstration that makes the point directly, or a statement challenging a common assumption the content then takes seriously."  
Cue: Most of the room will leave with one usable interrupt. Make them write it down against a piece they already have.  
---

### SLIDE 12 — CLICKBAIT AND THE USEFUL HOOK

\[10:06-11:10\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 12 / 13\. Claim, serif: Clickbait and a good hook look identical for three seconds. They differ in what happens after. Structure: a comparison ledger — clickbait and the useful hook matched row for row: the promise · what the content delivers · what the viewer learns about you · what happens on the second exposure, with the distrust row left lit on the clickbait column. Evidence: one promise broken beside the same promise kept, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 10 §10.12. Consequence, accent: The objective is not to be watched. It is to be trusted enough to be watched again.  
Purpose of this slide: Make the honesty rule governing every tool in the chapter explicit, and set up Chapter 11 (10.12).  
Say:  
"Clickbait and a useful hook can look the same. The difference is whether the opening honestly represents what follows.  
Clickbait opens a gap between the promise and the substance, using curiosity or emotion to generate engagement the content never justifies. A dramatic opening that does not deliver is clickbait, however well it gets the click.  
A useful hook creates genuine anticipation for something the content delivers. It may use any tool in this chapter — but whatever it promises is honoured.  
Clickbait accumulates distrust: viewers learn your openings cannot be relied on. A useful hook does the opposite — they learn that an interesting opening is worth trusting, because the content follows through. Every tool here answers to that rule: never manufacture attention the content does not deserve, but be trusted enough to be watched again."  
Cue: Do not soften this. The rule is the chapter's governing principle, and Chapter 11's workshop assumes it.  
---

### SLIDE 13 — CLOSE OF CHAPTER 10

\[11:10-12:00\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 13 / 13\. Claim, serif: Attention is earned in an order, and the order cannot be reversed. Structure: a statement card — the four gates resolved onto one line, in sequence: the frame · the first sentence · three seconds · relevance, with the chapter's opening frame still behind them. Evidence: the three questions from Slide 02 held at the foot as the test each gate must pass, provenance line From CAMERA Ch. 10 §10.2. Consequence, accent: Fix the opening first. Everything else in this programme is downstream of it.  
Purpose of this slide: Close the chapter, resolve the tools into an order, and hand the Day forward to hook construction.  
Say:  
"So attention is not a mystery and it is not luck. It is a sequence, and it runs in one direction: the frame, the first sentence, the first three seconds, then whether this applies to me.  
Four tools do the work of earning it — relevance, curiosity, tension, specificity — and one rule governs all of them: what you promise in the opening has to be what the content delivers.  
What you do not have yet is a repeatable way to construct an opening on demand. That is next: Chapter 11 takes these six ideas and turns them into hooks you can write in a workshop."  
Cue: Do not recap the tools one by one; the four gates on screen are the recap. Move to Chapter 11\.

## CHAPTER 10 — VISUAL AID SPECIFICATION (TASK 2 — PHASE D INPUT)

Status: nothing here is built. Section 8 puts visuals after the script is approved and after the Step A look gate. This chapter is specified to CAMERA\_V2/VISUALS/SLIDE-ARCHITECTURE.md, so each entry carries the five layers and names its component from the library, and every label on screen is 32 px or larger.  
The standard this chapter is written against. One self-contained HTML file, 1920 × 1080 stage that scales, no internet, system fonts only. Deep navy-black ground, off-white text, one muted gold accent, quiet steel for secondary text — never more than three colours on a slide. Serif for the claim and the figure that matters, clean sans elsewhere. Space or right arrow advances one build step, left arrow goes back, every animation ends in a stable final state, reduced motion shows the final states with no animation. Body text at least 44 px, labels and provenance at least 32 px, lines at least 3 px, 8% safe margin, CAMERA wordmark and slide number in the footer.  
The rule that applies to every slide here: it must demonstrate something that changes while the room watches. This chapter is about the first seconds of attention, so the demonstrations run a clock: two frames judged in one second, an opening sentence spent two ways, three seconds broken into what is being evaluated, a gap opened and left open, a familiar pattern scrolled past untouched.  
Techniques available from the style lock (approved look pending, so these are intended vocabulary, not a claim): canvas-filling SVG scenes rather than clip art; material built from gradients only — no glow, no blur, no drop shadow, no neon; a thin specular streak travelling a metal edge instead of an orbiting glow; demonstration by comparison, where two panels run the same process and diverge; live sorting, drifting or counting rather than static lists; and material held deliberately still where the claim is stability.  
Slide 01 — The Economics Of Attention. Type: Gate / flow with a cost ledger. Build: 3 steps. Component: gate / flow — the broadcast room against the feed, the same thirty-second window across both. Layers: chrome; claim, Attention is a finite budget, and every minute of your content is a bid against everything else on the screen.; the two columns and their exits; the cost ledger beneath, marked Illustrative; the consequence line. What changes: both columns open on the same thirty seconds; the ledger then runs the alternatives available in a commercial break against the alternatives available on the phone in front of them, the right-hand total climbing to a number too large to draw honestly; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the chapter's claim is an economy, and an economy is a comparison. The ledger is labelled Illustrative because the programme has no measured figure for it, and saying so is part of the argument — the point survives without an invented statistic.  
Slide 02 — Why People Stop Scrolling. Type: Scorecard — the three questions answered in a glance. Build: 3 steps. Component: scorecard, three rows the viewer answers instantly. Layers: chrome; claim, Nobody reads your content's contents page. They judge it in a fraction of a second.; the three rows; the same rows re-scored for a piece that was never watched; the consequence line. What changes: the three questions — does this apply to me · does this matter · is there a reason to keep watching — arrive one at a time and are marked answered by an unseen viewer; the second state re-runs them against a genuinely good piece and shows two rows unanswered; the third brings up the consequence line. Why: the subsection's claim is that a fraction of a second carries three judgements, and a scorecard is the only form that shows three verdicts at once without a list of bullets.  
Slide 03 — The First Frame. Type: Comparison ledger — two first frames, one second each. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger, matched rows. Layers: chrome; claim, Before you say a word, the first frame has already made your case — or lost it.; the two frames; the read test; the consequence line. What changes: two frames arrive side by side with the viewer's one-second read running against both; the matched rows — who is speaking · what environment · what is about to happen — then mark legible or unreadable on each; the third step dims the frame that failed and brings up the consequence line. Why: the teaching is that the frame already communicates, and matched rows are what make the comparison a judgement rather than a preference about lighting.  
Slide 04 — The First Sentence. Type: Cost ledger — the opening sentence spent two ways. Build: 3 steps. Component: cost ledger, running the same opening second down two paths. Layers: chrome; claim, Your first sentence is not an introduction. It is the reason someone decides to keep listening.; the two openings; the audience still present after each; the consequence line. What changes: the preamble is written out in full and struck through as the room watches the audience fall away; the relevant opening is then run against the same measure and holds; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the mistake this fixes is universal in the room, and writing the wrong opening out in full before striking it is what makes the fix feel obvious rather than theoretical.  
Slide 05 — The First Three Seconds. Type: Timeline with milestones — three seconds, four things evaluated. Build: 3 steps. Component: timeline with milestones across a three-second window. Layers: chrome; claim, Three seconds decide whether the next three minutes exist for anyone but you.; the window divided into what is evaluated at once; the same opening reviewed twice; the consequence line. What changes: the three-second window draws and splits into the frame · the first words · the tone · whether this fits me, all arriving together because that is the point; the segment spent on introductions is then marked as spent; the third step brings up the review question as the consequence line. Why: the claim is simultaneity inside a very short window, and a divided timeline shows simultaneity in a way a sequence cannot. The mark on the spent segment is what turns it into a habit.  
Slide 06 — Relevance. Type: 2 × 2 matrix — relevance stated against relevance felt. Build: 3 steps. Component: two-by-two matrix, axes general ↔ specific relevance and explicitly stated ↔ implicitly signalled. Layers: chrome; claim, Broadly related to your industry is not relevance. It is the reason nobody recognises themselves in your opening.; the four quadrants; the sample openings placed; the consequence line. What changes: the axes draw and the four quadrants fill with sample openings; two openings are then placed — one addressed to an industry, one to a situation the viewer is in today — and the second pulls while the first sits; the third step lights the specific-explicit quadrant and brings up the consequence line. Why: relevance is taught as a dial, and a matrix is the instrument that lets the room place its own last opening honestly.  
Slide 07 — Curiosity. Type: Quote panel — the gap stated, not closed. Build: 2 steps. Component: quote panel with the closing rule beneath. Layers: chrome; claim, Curiosity is a gap between what they know and what they want to know — and you have to be willing to fill it.; one honest gap on one line; the manufactured restatement beside it; the consequence line. What changes: the honest gap arrives and is deliberately left open with the rule the content must close it beneath; the manufactured version arrives beside it, its promise visibly larger than its payload, and brings up the consequence line. Why: two steps is the honest count — an open gap and a test, in that order. A third step would suggest a process the subsection does not describe.  
Slide 08 — Tension. Type: Ladder / stack — the problem built before the outcome. Build: 3 steps. Component: ladder / stack of one real situation. Layers: chrome; claim, Tension is not drama. It is an unresolved problem the viewer wants to see settled.; the rungs; the outcome withheld; the consequence line. What changes: a real customer situation climbs rung by rung — what could go wrong · what it costs · what was decided · how it ended — with the outcome held; the same situation is then replayed solution-first and loses its rise; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the teaching is an order of disclosure, and reversing it on the same material is the cheapest way to show a room why their case studies do not hold attention.  
Slide 09 — Specificity. Type: Evidence wall — specific claims landing. Build: 3 steps. Component: evidence wall of four matched pairs. Layers: chrome; claim, Specificity is the cheapest proof of experience you own, and generalities give it away for nothing.; the four pairs; the second phrasing marked as experience only this business could have; the consequence line. What changes: four pairs land one at a time — numbers · situations · timeframes · language — each showing the general phrase beside the specific one; the wall then holds only the specific column and marks it as ownable; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the subsection is a mechanical habit, and four paired examples make it a habit the room can run on its own copy tomorrow. The ownable column is the proof of experience made visible.  
Slide 10 — Stakes. Type: Decision bench — stakes stated against stakes inflated. Build: 3 steps. Component: decision bench, criteria as rows. Layers: chrome; claim, Consequence is what makes information worth attending to; without it, you are just describing things.; the two statements; the four rows; the consequence line. What changes: the same problem is stated abstractly and with its consequence as rows — time · money · safety · outcome — are judged; an inflated version is then placed beside it and loses on the same rows; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the ethical boundary of the chapter needs a demonstrated cost, not an instruction. Watching exaggeration lose the argument is what stops the room reaching for it.  
Slide 11 — Pattern Interrupts. Type: Timeline with milestones — pattern, interrupt, pattern. Build: 3 steps. Component: timeline with milestones across a scroll. Layers: chrome; claim, Viewers have learned to scroll past you; the only way past that is to be visibly not the pattern.; the familiar pattern untouched; two interrupts matched against what follows; the consequence line. What changes: a familiar piece scrolls past untouched; an interrupt then lands and holds the scroll; a second interrupt is placed beside it and matched against the content that follows, one honoured and one not; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the condition of use is the lesson, and the only way to show it is to put two interrupts next to two different follow-throughs.  
Slide 12 — Clickbait And The Useful Hook. Type: Comparison ledger — clickbait and the hook, matched row for row. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger, four matched rows. Layers: chrome; claim, Clickbait and a good hook look identical for three seconds. They differ in what happens after.; the four rows; the second exposure; the consequence line. What changes: the two columns fill across the promise · what the content delivers · what the viewer learns about you · what happens on the second exposure; the clickbait column's trust row then falls on the second exposure while the hook's holds; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the difference between the two is invisible on first contact and obvious on second, so the slide has to run the second exposure. It is also the chapter's governing rule, and it closes the Engagement block's teaching.  
Slide 13 — Close Of Chapter 10\. Type: Statement card — the four gates, resolved. Build: 3 steps. Component: statement card echoing Slide 01, with the gates resolving. Layers: chrome; claim, Attention is earned in an order, and the order cannot be reversed.; the four gates; the three questions held at the foot; the consequence line. What changes: the chapter's opening frame returns in its opening typography; the four gates resolve onto one line — the frame · the first sentence · three seconds · relevance; the third step holds the three questions from Slide 02 at the foot as the test each gate passes, and brings up the consequence line. Why: closing in the opening's visual language tells the room the unit is finished, and an order is the recall device for a chapter about a sequence. Holding the three questions at the foot hands that test forward to Chapter 11\.  
Supplementary — the three-second audit (place alongside Slide 05). Type: workshop frame. Build: 1 step. What changes: nothing after the reveal — the frame names the one-minute audit: play your own opening, stop at three seconds, and mark each of the four evaluations as answered or unanswered. Why: it converts the chapter into something the room can run on its own published content that evening. Chapter 10 carries no live exercise — the Day's 20 minutes are fully allocated — so if this is used in live time it is charged against the Day's interaction budget and traded out of another exercise rather than added on top; as homework it costs the Day nothing.

## CHAPTER 11 — HOOK CONSTRUCTION

### SLIDE 01 — THE HOOK LIBRARY

\[0:00-0:32\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 01 / 13\. Claim, serif: A hook is not a style. It is the specific opening that puts the principles to work. Structure: a decision bench — the eleven structures as rows, judged against four columns: names the viewer's situation · creates a gap · needs proof · fits which stage of the journey. Evidence: the four columns marked from the chapter's own material, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 11\. Consequence, accent: Choose the structure your material can actually support, not the one that sounds boldest.  
Purpose of this slide: Frame the chapter as a library of structures rather than a theory, and set the selection rule the close returns to.  
Say:  
"The last chapter gave you the principles: relevance, curiosity, tension, specificity. This one turns them into openings you can use.  
A hook is the specific opening statement, question or moment that puts those principles to work on a real piece.  
You will not use all eleven structures that follow. Most businesses find three or four that fit their subject, their audience and how they naturally speak."  
Cue: Say plainly that this is a library, not a checklist. The room should leave with three structures it can use this week, not eleven it has heard of.  
---

### SLIDE 02 — THE PROBLEM HOOK

\[0:32-1:09\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 02 / 13\. Claim, serif: Name the problem your viewer is living with, and the right person stops. Structure: a comparison ledger — two problem openings matched row for row: what it names · who recognises themselves · whether it sounds personal. Evidence: the broad version and the specific version side by side, the second marked as the one a portion of the audience recognises instantly, provenance line From your Chapter 6 audience profile. Consequence, accent: The opening does not have to solve the problem. It has to make the right person stop.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the structure that all the others are variations on, and its dependence on specificity (11.1).  
Say:  
"The problem hook names a specific problem the audience is living with, before any solution appears.  
It draws on the audience diagnosis you already have: someone with that exact problem has an immediate reason to stay.  
Specificity is everything. Struggling with your marketing is too broad to be anyone's situation; posting every week and the phone never ringing is instantly recognisable.  
The opening does not need to solve it. It needs to make the right person stop."  
Cue: Point at the specific version on screen and stop talking for a beat. The room recognises itself in that line, and that recognition is the lesson.  
---

### SLIDE 03 — THE QUESTION HOOK

\[1:09-1:45\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 03 / 13\. Claim, serif: A question makes them answer. That is the whole mechanism. Structure: a scorecard — three tests a question must pass: applies to a real subset · is honest about what follows · invites reflection rather than reflex, marked on a working question and on a failing one. Evidence: Do you want more customers scored against the same three, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 11 §11.2. Consequence, accent: If your question gets an automatic yes, it is not a question — it is a formality.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the room the mechanism and the test for the commonest weak hook (11.2).  
Say:  
"The question hook opens with a direct question, which prompts an answer in the viewer's head before you have delivered anything.  
Even a brief, almost unconscious yes, no or not sure is participation, and participation is engagement. A statement asks for nothing.  
A working question applies to a real subset of your audience and is honestly answered by the content.  
Do you want more customers gets an automatic yes and no reflection at all."  
Cue: Ask the room to write one question they would genuinely ask their audience — not one they would ask a market. The distinction is the exercise this chapter does not have time for.  
---

### SLIDE 04 — THE STATEMENT HOOK

\[1:45-2:27\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 04 / 13\. Claim, serif: Say the conclusion first; the explanation is what they stay for. Structure: a quote panel — the claim set alone and plainly, with the support test beneath it: can you prove this in the next thirty seconds? Evidence: a workable claim and the same claim pushed until it strains belief, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 11 §11.3. Consequence, accent: Strong enough to be worth stating plainly, never so extreme that it strains belief before you have offered any support.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach conclusion-before-reasoning as the mechanism, and its ceiling (11.3).  
Say:  
"The statement hook opens with a direct claim, often against a common assumption, and does not justify it yet.  
Conclusion before reasoning creates the curiosity: the natural response to an unexplained claim is wanting to know why it is true, which carries the viewer into the explanation.  
The claim has to be one you can support. Most businesses lose customers to confusion rather than price works if what follows proves it.  
That is the calibration: strong enough to be worth saying, not so extreme that it strains belief."  
Cue: This structure is the easiest to abuse. Say that the claim is a promise, and the next thirty seconds are the payment.  
---

### SLIDE 05 — THE CONTRARIAN HOOK

\[2:27-3:05\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 05 / 13\. Claim, serif: Challenging a belief buys tension — but only if you have the substance to pay for it. Structure: a gate / flow — a common belief entering the gate, with two exits: supported by your own experience and asserted to look bold, the second exit visibly failing. Evidence: the two exits marked against one piece of standard advice in the business's own field, provenance line From your own experience, or labelled Illustrative if the example is constructed. Consequence, accent: Disagree only where you have watched the standard advice fail.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the structure its honest condition of use (11.4).  
Say:  
"The contrarian hook challenges a belief or a piece of standard advice your audience probably holds.  
It creates productive tension. Hold the belief and you want to see how the disagreement is justified; already suspect it and you want confirmation.  
It needs real substance. Disagreeing with something popular to look bold is seen through fast and costs credibility; the strongest versions come from watching the advice fail yourself.  
Not every subject deserves it, and manufactured disagreement reads as insincere."  
Cue: Name the failure mode out loud — a contrarian hook written because the format performs, not because the business believes it.  
---

### SLIDE 06 — THE STORY HOOK

\[3:05-3:44\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 06 / 13\. Claim, serif: Begin inside the story, not before it. Structure: a timeline with milestones — one customer story laid along a line, with the two possible entry points marked: where the business usually starts and where the situation is already moving. Evidence: the same story opened at both points, with the second arriving inside the first two sentences, provenance line From your own case history. Consequence, accent: Start at the interesting part. Context is what you spend after attention is earned.  
Purpose of this slide: Move the story's start point, which is the whole discipline of the structure (11.5).  
Say:  
"The story hook drops the viewer into a specific situation, often mid-action.  
Stories hold attention better than statements, and the point of this structure is to begin inside one rather than eventually arrive at one. A customer called us in a panic last week because puts the viewer straight into a situation with stakes.  
The discipline is where you start: close to the interesting part.  
Lengthy context before the point is how a story loses the viewer before it becomes worth hearing."  
Cue: If the room remembers one structural fix from this chapter, it should be this one — the setup they currently open with.  
---

### SLIDE 07 — THE DEMONSTRATION HOOK

\[3:44-4:23\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 07 / 13\. Claim, serif: Show the thing. Do not describe the thing you are about to show. Structure: a comparison ledger — two openings for one video matched row for row: what the viewer sees in the first three seconds · what they have to be told · what holds their eye. Evidence: describing-then-showing against showing-then-explaining, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 11 §11.6. Consequence, accent: Start at the most visually interesting moment you have, not at the logical beginning of the process.  
Purpose of this slide: Move the start point from the logical beginning to the interesting one (11.6).  
Say:  
"The demonstration hook starts by showing something happening instead of describing what is about to be shown.  
It suits visual subjects: a process, a comparison, a before and after. The video simply begins demonstrating, and the picture earns the first seconds on its own.  
Start at the most visually interesting moment you have, not the logical beginning. A repair video can open where the problem becomes visible, not with arriving at the site.  
Context can follow once the picture has earned attention."  
Cue: The room will argue that context is needed first. Answer that context is what a viewer asks for after they decide to stay.  
---

### SLIDE 08 — THE MISTAKE HOOK

\[4:23-5:02\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 08 / 13\. Claim, serif: Tell them the thing they are doing is a mistake — and be specific enough to be believed. Structure: an evidence wall — named mistakes landing one at a time, each marked common enough to matter or too rare to land. Evidence: one specific mistake and one obscure one, with only the first marked as creating recognition, provenance line From your own records, or labelled Illustrative if the count is not verified. Consequence, accent: A rare error creates no recognition, and no recognition means no hook.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the mistake structure its specificity test, and add the recognition test (11.7).  
Say:  
"The mistake hook names a specific, common mistake the audience is likely making, often without knowing it.  
Being told that something you believed was right is wrong gives a strong reason to stay, both to understand why and to find out whether it applies to you.  
It has to be specific and genuinely common. Most people clean this the wrong way, and it makes the problem worse is credible and personal.  
A rare error creates no recognition, so it creates no hook."  
Cue: Ask the room to name the mistake it corrects most often. Whatever comes back easiest is the one that is common enough to open with.  
---

### SLIDE 09 — THE "YOU ARE DOING THIS WRONG" STRUCTURE

\[5:02-5:41\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 09 / 13\. Claim, serif: The accusation is free. The correction is the content. Structure: a ladder / stack — the accusation on the lower rung and the specific alternative above it, with the rung missing in a version that is all accusation and no correction. Evidence: the same structure run with and without its alternative, matched to two different Characters, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 11 §11.8, and your Day 1 Character work. Consequence, accent: An accusation with no clear alternative is not content — it is just an accusation.  
Purpose of this slide: Set the tone condition and the structural requirement at once (11.8).  
Say:  
"This is the mistake hook stated directly: you tell the viewer their current approach is wrong, then explain what to do instead.  
It is more confrontational, so it has to match the Character you established on Day 1\. A direct, authoritative voice carries it; a warmer one is better served by softer phrasing around the same content.  
Whatever the tone, the structure stands on the correction that follows.  
An accusation with no clear alternative is not content, it is just an accusation."  
Cue: Point back at their Character work. The structure is not forbidden to a warm brand; it just has to be delivered in their voice.  
---

### SLIDE 10 — THE "BEFORE YOU DO X" STRUCTURE

\[5:41-6:22\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 10 / 13\. Claim, serif: Catch them at the decision, not at the subject. Structure: a timeline with milestones — a real purchase decision drawn as a line, with the moment the customer is already planning the action marked and the information they need placed before it. Evidence: one decision the business's own customers make, with what they typically overlook at that stage, provenance line From the Chapter 8 revenue map. Consequence, accent: Write to a moment in their process, not to a topic in your field.  
Purpose of this slide: Connect the hook library back to the Monetization work, and to decision-stage content (11.9).  
Say:  
"This structure addresses the viewer at a specific decision point, giving them what they need before an action they are already planning.  
It is built for decision-stage content, because it speaks to someone choosing something right now. Before you sign the lease on your next location is a real moment in a real process, and relevance rarely gets sharper.  
Writing it requires knowing which decisions your audience makes, and what they overlook at that stage.  
That comes from the decision-content work in the Monetization chapters."  
Cue: This is the structure that connects this chapter to Day 2's earlier half. Say so, then move — the room has the map already.  
---

### SLIDE 11 — THE AUTHORITY HOOK

\[6:22-7:01\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 11 / 13\. Claim, serif: One sentence of standing, then straight into the substance. Structure: a cost ledger — the same opening second spent two ways: a credential biography against one relevant credential and the claim, with the second marked as already into the substance. Evidence: a one-sentence authority line and the extended version beside it, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 11 §11.10. Consequence, accent: The experience you cite has to bear on the specific claim that follows.  
Purpose of this slide: Rescue the legitimate use of credentials while keeping the opening fast (11.10).  
Say:  
"The authority hook establishes briefly why you are placed to speak on this subject, then moves straight into it.  
Keep it to a sentence. An extended credential introduction is the slow opening the last chapter warned about. After inspecting several hundred of these systems, here is the one thing that predicts failure establishes standing and is already into the substance.  
The authority must relate to the specific claim that follows.  
General experience, disconnected from the point, spends seconds without buying credibility."  
Cue: This is the structure owners reach for first and overuse most. Say that relevance, not length, is what buys credibility.  
---

### SLIDE 12 — THE CURIOSITY GAP

\[7:01-7:41\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 12 / 13\. Claim, serif: Withhold one specific thing — then actually deliver it. Structure: an annotated chart — anticipation drawn across a piece from the promise to the payoff, with the point where the answer must land marked, and an unresolved version left visibly hanging. Evidence: one gap opened and closed, beside one opened and never closed, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 11 §11.11. Consequence, accent: A gap you never close is clickbait, and the last chapter has already priced that.  
Purpose of this slide: Close the chapter's teaching with the technique that layers onto all the others, and its honesty rule (11.11).  
Say:  
"The curiosity gap is less a structure than a technique you layer on. You withhold one specific thing the viewer wants, while making clear it is coming.  
There is one mistake that causes most of the failures we see, and it is not what you would expect promises something specific without delivering it yet.  
Used honestly it is among your strongest tools. Used carelessly it is clickbait: an answer never properly delivered, or unremarkable after the build-up, spends trust instead of earning it."  
Cue: Do not let this slide read as a licence to tease. The rule from the last chapter is the frame, and the payoff has to be worth the wait.  
---

### SLIDE 13 — CLOSE OF CHAPTER 11

\[7:41-8:20\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 2 · E: ENGAGEMENT · 13 / 13\. Claim, serif: Three or four structures will fit you. Find them by writing, not by thinking. Structure: a statement card — the eleven structures collapsed onto one line, with the three or four the business keeps held above the others. Evidence: the selection rule from the chapter's own material, provenance line Source: CAMERA Ch. 11, closing section. Consequence, accent: Write several openings for the same piece and watch which one earns attention from the audience you actually have.  
Purpose of this slide: Close the chapter, hand the room the selection rule, and hand the Day forward to retention.  
Say:  
"Treat these as starting points, not a formula. A business usually finds three or four that fit its Character and its audience, and those are the ones worth returning to.  
The way to find out which is not to think about it. Write several openings for the same piece and watch which one earns attention from the audience you actually have.  
That is where Chapter 12 begins: what to do once the hook has worked and the viewer is still there."  
Cue: Do not recap the eleven structures; the collapsed line on screen is the recap. Move to Chapter 12\.

## CHAPTER 11 — VISUAL AID SPECIFICATION (TASK 2 — PHASE D INPUT)

Status: nothing here is built. Section 8 puts visuals after the script is approved and after the Step A look gate. Specified to CAMERA\_V2/VISUALS/SLIDE-ARCHITECTURE.md, with every label at 32 px or larger and the five layers named on every slide.  
The rule that applies to every slide here: it must demonstrate something that changes while the room watches. Eleven hook structures could easily become eleven copies of one comparison, so this chapter varies the instrument deliberately: a decision bench for the library, matched ledgers where two openings differ, a gate where a belief fails its test, timelines where only the start point moves, an evidence wall where recognition does or does not arrive, and one annotated chart for the gap. No slide in this chapter asks for a number the source does not contain, so no chart is fabricated and the two constructed examples carry the Illustrative label.  
Slide 01 — The Hook Library. Type: Decision bench — the eleven structures against four criteria. Build: 3 steps. Component: decision bench, structures as rows and four criteria as columns. Layers: chrome; claim, A hook is not a style. It is the specific opening that puts the principles to work.; the bench filling structure by structure; the four criteria marked from the chapter's own material; the consequence line. What changes: the eleven rows arrive in three groups; the four columns then mark each row; the third step brings up the selection line and dims the rows the chapter will not return to. Why: the chapter is a library, and a library is only useful if the room can see which shelf to take from. Building the bench before the structures are taught gives the room a place to file each one as it arrives.  
Slide 02 — The Problem Hook. Type: Comparison ledger — a broad problem against a recognizable one. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger, three matched rows. Layers: chrome; claim, Name the problem your viewer is living with, and the right person stops.; the two openings; the three rows marked; the consequence line. What changes: both openings arrive and the rows mark what it names · who recognises themselves · whether it sounds personal; the specific version is then shown landing with a segment of the audience while the broad one lands with nobody; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the whole structure depends on specificity, and specificity is only visible as a comparison with its opposite. The recognition is demonstrated rather than asserted.  
Slide 03 — The Question Hook. Type: Scorecard — three tests a question must pass. Build: 3 steps. Component: scorecard, three rows against two sample questions. Layers: chrome; claim, A question makes them answer. That is the whole mechanism.; the three tests; both questions scored; the consequence line. What changes: the three tests arrive — applies to a real subset · honest about what follows · invites reflection rather than reflex; a working question is scored against them; the third step scores Do you want more customers, which fails all three and brings up the consequence line. Why: the commonest weak hook in the room is a rhetorical question, and a scorecard is the only instrument that shows it failing without the presenter having to criticise anyone's work.  
Slide 04 — The Statement Hook. Type: Quote panel — the claim stated plainly, with its support test. Build: 3 steps. Component: quote panel with a test beneath it. Layers: chrome; claim, Say the conclusion first; the explanation is what they stay for.; the claim set alone; the support test; the consequence line. What changes: the claim arrives alone and deliberately unjustified; the test — can you prove this in the next thirty seconds? — then appears beneath it; the third step shows the same claim pushed until it strains belief and brings up the consequence line. Why: the mechanism is that an unexplained claim creates the reason to stay, so the claim must be shown alone before anything justifies it. The pushed version is what calibrates the ceiling.  
Slide 05 — The Contrarian Hook. Type: Gate / flow — the belief challenged, and the substance test. Build: 3 steps. Component: gate / flow with two exits. Layers: chrome; claim, Challenging a belief buys tension — but only if you have the substance to pay for it.; the belief entering the gate; the two exits; the consequence line. What changes: a piece of standard advice enters the gate; the exit marked supported by your own experience opens and carries the piece forward; the third step runs the same advice through the exit marked asserted to look bold, which visibly fails, and brings up the consequence line. Why: the structure's condition of use is the lesson, and a gate shows a condition being met and missed on identical input. It also gives the presenter somewhere to stand when the room wants to disagree with something for effect.  
Slide 06 — The Story Hook. Type: Timeline with milestones — where the story starts. Build: 3 steps. Component: timeline with milestones along one customer story. Layers: chrome; claim, Begin inside the story, not before it.; the story as a line; the two entry points; the consequence line. What changes: the story is laid along a line; the entry point most businesses use is marked and the viewer visibly leaves before the interesting part; the third step moves the entry point into the situation already in motion and brings up the consequence line. Why: the only thing this structure changes is a start point, and a start point is a position on a line. Watching the viewer leave before the good part is what makes the fix feel necessary.  
Slide 07 — The Demonstration Hook. Type: Comparison ledger — describing against showing. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger, three matched rows. Layers: chrome; claim, Show the thing. Do not describe the thing you are about to show.; the two openings; the rows marked; the consequence line. What changes: two openings for one video arrive, one describing and one showing; the rows mark what the viewer sees in the first three seconds · what they have to be told · what holds their eye; the third step holds both frames side by side and brings up the consequence line. Why: a demonstration hook is defined by what happens instead of an introduction, and the comparison is what makes that substitution visible. Holding both frames is the whole argument in one state.  
Slide 08 — The Mistake Hook. Type: Evidence wall — the mistake named, and who recognises themselves. Build: 3 steps. Component: evidence wall of named mistakes, each marked for how common it is. Layers: chrome; claim, Tell them the thing they are doing is a mistake — and be specific enough to be believed.; the mistakes landing; the recognition marks; the consequence line. What changes: mistakes arrive one at a time and are marked common enough to matter or too rare to land; an obscure error is shown drawing no recognition at all; the third step clears everything but the specific mistake and brings up the consequence line. Why: the structure runs on recognition, and recognition is something the room can watch arrive or not arrive on a wall of examples. The obscure error is the honest control.  
Slide 09 — The "You Are Doing This Wrong" Structure. Type: Ladder / stack — the accusation and the correction. Build: 3 steps. Component: ladder / stack with the accusation below and the alternative above. Layers: chrome; claim, The accusation is free. The correction is the content.; the ladder; the two Characters; the consequence line. What changes: the accusation arrives on the lower rung; the specific alternative is then built on the rung above it and the structure holds; the third step runs the version with no alternative — all accusation, nothing above it — and brings up the consequence line. Why: the requirement is a rung that must exist, and a stack shows the structure failing when it is missing. The same content is also run in a warm voice and a direct one, so the tone condition is demonstrated rather than instructed.  
Slide 10 — The "Before You Do X" Structure. Type: Timeline with milestones — the decision point in the journey. Build: 3 steps. Component: timeline with milestones across a real purchase decision. Layers: chrome; claim, Catch them at the decision, not at the subject.; the decision line; the overlooked information; the consequence line. What changes: a decision the business's customers actually make is drawn as a line; the moment the customer is already planning the action is marked; the third step places the information they need just before that mark and brings up the consequence line. Why: the structure is defined by a position in someone else's process, and only a timeline puts that position where the room can see it. It also ties the hook library back to Day 2's revenue map.  
Slide 11 — The Authority Hook. Type: Cost ledger — one sentence of standing against an extended biography. Build: 3 steps. Component: cost ledger, running the same opening second two ways. Layers: chrome; claim, One sentence of standing, then straight into the substance.; the two openings; the seconds spent; the consequence line. What changes: the credential biography is shown consuming the opening while the substance has not started; the one-sentence version is then run and is already into the claim; the third step shows a credential unrelated to the claim buying no credibility, and brings up the consequence line. Why: the failure is a cost, and a cost is best shown as seconds spent. The unrelated credential is the case most rooms are actually in.  
Slide 12 — The Curiosity Gap. Type: Annotated chart — the gap opened and closed. Build: 3 steps. Component: annotated chart of anticipation across a piece. Layers: chrome; claim, Withhold one specific thing — then actually deliver it.; the anticipation curve; where the answer must land; the consequence line. What changes: anticipation is drawn from the promise forward; the point where the answer must land is marked and the curve falls away as it is delivered; the third step runs a gap that is never closed, where the curve simply decays, and brings up the consequence line. Why: withholding is the one technique in the chapter whose effect runs over time and whose failure is invisible statically. The unresolved version is the last chapter's clickbait distinction, drawn.  
Slide 13 — Close Of Chapter 11\. Type: Statement card — the library resolved, with the selection rule. Build: 3 steps. Component: statement card echoing Slide 01\. Layers: chrome; claim, Three or four structures will fit you. Find them by writing, not by thinking.; the eleven collapsed onto one line; the three or four held above it; the consequence line. What changes: the chapter's opening bench returns and the eleven structures collapse onto a single line; the three or four the business keeps rise above it; the third step holds the selection rule and brings up the consequence line. Why: closing in the opening's visual language tells the room the unit is finished, and collapsing eleven into one line is the recall device. It also hands the Day forward to retention without recapping the structures one by one.  
Supplementary — the hook ledger (place alongside Slide 13). Type: workshop frame. Build: 1 step. What changes: nothing after the reveal — the frame names the one-hour task: take one piece already planned, write four openings for it using four different structures from the library, and record which one the audience responds to. Why: the chapter has no exercise because the Day's 20 minutes are spent and because §11.13 Hook Workshop was dropped from the coverage map with no source text to teach from, so this is the smallest honest substitute, and it is homework rather than live time. It is also the only way the room finds out which three structures are theirs, which is what the close asks them to do.
