\[0:00-0:41\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 01 / 18\. Claim, serif: The tool is not the point. The method around it is. Structure: a ladder / stack — the Day's closing method in six rungs: give it context · brief it properly · iterate · use it as a critic · verify · capture the template, the last rung lit as the one that makes the other five repeatable. Evidence: the prediction-not-understanding rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30, opening. Consequence, accent: Feed it what it does not know — then check what it gives back.  
Purpose of this slide: Open the chapter's craft and set up the Day's close (intro).  
Say:  
"Chapter 29 was about where AI belongs in the workflow. This chapter is about how to actually work with it — the craft of getting useful output out of a tool that predicts the next plausible word rather than knowing anything.  
It is also Day 4's last chapter, so it closes the Day as well. Everything we have built today comes together here as one working method.  
And that method starts with a single fact: these tools are only ever as good as what you put in."  
Cue: The six rungs are the chapter; the lit one is where tonight's homework comes from.

### SLIDE 02 — WHAT AN LLM ACTUALLY DOES (30.1)

\[0:41-1:37\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 02 / 18\. Claim, serif: It predicts the next plausible word — it does not know, and it does not think. Structure: a comparison ledger — what it does against what it does not do, matched on the same system: generates fluent, well-organised, often useful language on one side; knows facts, thinks, or raises an alarm when it does not know, on the other. Evidence: the prediction-not-understanding rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.1. Consequence, accent: Treat fluency as style, never as proof.  
Purpose of this slide: Establish the one fact the rest of the chapter follows from (30.1).  
Say:  
"A large language model does one thing at its core: it predicts the next most probable piece of text, based on everything before it in the conversation, trained on enormous quantities of text.  
It does not know facts the way a person knows facts, and it does not think the way a person thinks. Its output is often useful and well organised, because plausible language depends on being accurate and coherent. But the mechanism underneath is prediction, not understanding, and every other principle here follows from that.  
It will produce a wrong answer with exactly the fluency it produces a right one, and no internal alarm fires when it does not know. Catching that stays your job."  
Cue: The two columns are the chapter's foundation; everything after this slide is a consequence of this one.

### SLIDE 03 — CONTEXT (30.2)

\[1:37-2:33\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 03 / 18\. Claim, serif: The single biggest lever you hold — and the one most people never pull. Structure: a ladder / stack — the context ladder, five rungs climbing from a vague request through your positioning · the specific audience · examples in your voice · the platform and the outcome wanted, output quality climbing with each rung. Evidence: the quality-bound-to-context rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.2. Consequence, accent: Most disappointing output is missing context, not a weak tool.  
Purpose of this slide: Make context the chapter's central discipline (30.2).  
Say:  
"An LLM only knows what has been provided in the current conversation, plus the general patterns it absorbed during training. It does not know your voice, your last five years of client work, or what you finished yesterday — unless you tell it.  
That is context, and the quality of everything it produces is bound directly to the quality and completeness of the context it is given: your positioning, the specific audience, examples of past work in your voice, and the outcome you want.  
This is the single biggest lever you hold over AI-assisted work, and the lever most people never learn to pull. Most disappointing output traces back to missing context, not a limitation of the tool."  
Cue: Climb the rungs in order; the top rung is the request that reads as though it were written for you.

### SLIDE 04 — PROMPTING (30.3)

\[2:33-3:28\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 04 / 18\. Claim, serif: A prompt is a brief — and a brief has four parts. Structure: a comparison ledger — a vague ask against a briefed ask, matched on the same four rows: the task · who it is for · the format · what to avoid. Evidence: the four-part-prompt rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.3. Consequence, accent: Brief it like a freelancer who cannot ask you questions.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the four things every prompt must carry (30.3).  
Say:  
"A prompt is the instruction you give the tool, and prompting is the skill of writing it so the model produces what you actually need. It is not a technical skill. It is closer to briefing a talented freelancer who knows nothing about your business and cannot ask follow-up questions unless you invite them.  
A strong prompt identifies four things: what the task is, who the output is for, what format it should take, and what should be avoided.  
'Write a social post about our new service' produces something usable and generic. Specify the platform, the audience's pain point, your tone and the call to action, and you get something dramatically closer to final."  
Cue: The four rows are the instrument; say them slowly enough that the room writes them down.

### SLIDE 05 — PROVIDING SOURCE MATERIAL (30.4)

\[3:28-4:23\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 05 / 18\. Claim, serif: Real material beats a good description of the material, every time. Structure: an evidence wall — the source folder filling with what a business already owns: a client conversation transcript · raw notes · a past post in your voice · a customer review · a competitor's post, with the empty cells left visible. Evidence: the anchors-to-something-real rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.4. Consequence, accent: Keep the folder ready; paste instead of describing.  
Purpose of this slide: Make supplied material the default, not the exception (30.4).  
Say:  
"The most reliable way to raise the quality of the output is to hand the model real source material rather than asking it to generate from nothing.  
That might be a transcript of a client conversation, an existing piece of content in your voice, or a customer review. Source material anchors the output to something real and specific rather than letting the model fall back on generic patterns from its training data.  
The habit worth building: keep a small folder of representative material ready to paste — a few strong past posts, your positioning, a sample of real customer language. That turns every session into a continuation of established work rather than a cold start."  
Cue: The empty cells are the point; the folder has to be filled before it is needed.

### SLIDE 06 — GIVING THE AI A JOB (30.5)

\[4:23-5:16\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 06 / 18\. Claim, serif: Give it a role, and it reviews your work through eyes that are not yours. Structure: a decision bench — a draft held centrally with two exits: read it as yourself and read it as a named role — a first-time visitor, a skeptical customer, an experienced copyeditor, each labelled with what that lens catches and what it misses. Evidence: the narrows-the-patterns rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.5. Consequence, accent: Assign the role, then ask what is wrong.  
Purpose of this slide: Use the role technique where your own eyes are the problem (30.5).  
Say:  
"One of the more effective techniques is to assign the model a specific job before asking for the task: an experienced copyeditor, a skeptical potential customer, a social media strategist reviewing a draft.  
This is not a magic trick. It works because it narrows the range of patterns the model draws from, focusing its output on the conventions, vocabulary and priorities of that role.  
It is most useful when a piece needs evaluating from a perspective that is not yours. Ask the model to review your copy as a first-time visitor who has never heard of your business, and it will surface confusion you, who already know everything, would never notice."  
Cue: The value is the second exit; a role catches what knowing too much blinds you to.

### SLIDE 07 — GIVING THE AI CONSTRAINTS (30.6)

\[5:16-6:08\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 07 / 18\. Claim, serif: Constraints are not a limit on creativity. They are what makes the output usable. Structure: a cost ledger — the same piece run twice: an unconstrained draft with the model's defaults filling every gap, and its editing cost per section against the constrained draft written to a maximum count, a required tone, a banned list and a required structure. Evidence: the constrain-up-front rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.6. Consequence, accent: Set the boundary before the draft, not after it.  
Purpose of this slide: Move constraints upstream of the draft (30.6).  
Say:  
"Constraints are the boundaries around a task: length limits, tone requirements, words and phrases to avoid, platform rules, formatting requirements, things that must not be said.  
They are not a limit on creativity. They are what turns an open-ended, generic response into a usable one. An unconstrained request invites the model to fill every gap with its own default assumptions, which tend toward the generic.  
Useful constraints: a maximum count matched to the platform, a required tone, a banned-word list, a required structure, and any legal, brand or factual boundary. Setting them up front is far more efficient than producing an unconstrained draft and editing it down afterwards."  
Cue: The two columns are the section; the unconstrained column's editing hours are the argument.

### SLIDE 08 — ITERATION (30.7)

\[6:08-7:04\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 08 / 18\. Claim, serif: Specific feedback, not a new prompt, is what closes the gap. Structure: a timeline with milestones — the draft's three revision cycles on one rule: the first response · 'make it better', which changes little · the targeted instruction — cut a third, drop the second paragraph, open with a question, the cost of each cycle falling as the direction tightens. Evidence: the specific-feedback rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.7. Consequence, accent: Never restart what you can re-direct.  
Purpose of this slide: Make iteration specific, and keep the conversation alive (30.7).  
Say:  
"The first response should rarely be treated as final. Iteration is reviewing that draft, identifying specifically what is wrong or missing, and asking for a revision that addresses those points — rather than starting over with a new prompt, because the model retains the conversation's context and can adjust rather than regenerate.  
Effective iteration is specific. 'Make it better' gives it almost nothing to act on. 'Cut this by a third, remove the second paragraph, and make the opening line a question' gives it exact direction.  
It applies to structure too: ask for three different opening lines, or two approaches to the same piece, and choose or combine. That costs a follow-up prompt, not another drafting session."  
Cue: The falling cost per cycle is the teaching; vague feedback is what makes this slow.

### SLIDE 09 — CRITICISM AND REVISION (30.8)

\[7:04-8:02\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 09 / 18\. Claim, serif: Ask for praise and you get praise. Ask for the weaknesses, and it earns its keep. Structure: a gate / flow — a draft arriving at a critic's gate by one of two requests: 'review this', which passes a safe generic approval, and 'find the three biggest weaknesses and explain why each is one', which leaves no room for the safe answer. Evidence: the ask-for-problems rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.8. Consequence, accent: Use it as a pressure test — not as a second opinion you can hide behind.  
Purpose of this slide: Turn the tool into a critic rather than a publisher (30.8).  
Say:  
"Beyond correcting a draft, the tool can be used deliberately as a critic — asked to identify weaknesses in a piece before it goes out, rather than only to produce it.  
This needs a different prompt from drafting: one that asks for problems rather than praise. Prompt it to 'review this' and you will often get generic approval, because approval is the safe answer. Prompt it to 'find the three biggest weaknesses in this draft and explain why each is one' and you get something useful, because the instruction leaves no room for the safe one.  
It is not a substitute for human judgment — the model has no stake in your business. It is a pressure test before material goes public."  
Cue: The two exits are the choice; the vague one is the default the room falls into.

### SLIDE 10 — FACT CHECKING (30.9)

\[8:02-8:58\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 10 / 18\. Claim, serif: Nothing in the output tells you whether it is true. Structure: a gate / flow — a specific claim arriving at a verification gate with two exits: independently confirmed and published because it read plausibly, the second tagged with the specifics it most often gets wrong — names, numbers, dates, industry and competitor claims, your own results and credentials. Evidence: the unverified-until-checked rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.9. Consequence, accent: Assume every specific is unverified until you check it.  
Purpose of this slide: Make fact-checking the final non-negotiable step (30.9).  
Say:  
"Because the model generates plausible language rather than verified truth, any factual claim, statistic, quote or specific detail it produces has to be checked before it is published: names, numbers, dates and anything presented as established fact.  
It can produce an incorrect statistic with exactly the fluent, confident tone it uses for a correct one, and there is no built-in signal that distinguishes the two.  
So assume anything specific and checkable in a draft is unverified until you verify it independently. That matters most for claims about your own results, credentials or history, where the tool has no real information at all. Treat the check as non-negotiable, exactly as a professional writer treats it with any source."  
Cue: Chapter 29 drew this gate for research; here it is the last step of every draft, not one stage of the workflow.

### SLIDE 11 — MAINTAINING PERSONAL VOICE (30.10)

\[8:58-9:54\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 11 / 18\. Claim, serif: Show it three paragraphs of your voice — do not describe the voice. Structure: a comparison ledger — describing the voice against showing the voice, matched on what each gives the model to imitate: 'friendly but professional' in the abstract on one side; three real paragraphs of your own writing or speech on the other, with the final human pass on both. Evidence: the show-don't-describe rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.10. Consequence, accent: Read it back — would you say it out loud, to a real client?  
Purpose of this slide: Make voice a supplied sample plus a human pass (30.10).  
Say:  
"Left with a generic prompt, the model defaults to a generic voice: competent, correct, and interchangeable with any other business in your category.  
Maintaining your actual voice is not automatic. Supply real examples of your own writing or speech as source material, and instruct the model to match the tone, sentence rhythm and vocabulary of those examples. Describing a voice in the abstract — 'friendly but professional' — is far weaker than showing three real paragraphs written in your own voice.  
And even with strong source material, read every draft yourself and ask whether you would actually say it that way, out loud, to a real client. Where you would not, that is a direct edit — not another iteration."  
Cue: The final human pass is not optional; voice is the one thing the tool can only approximate.

### SLIDE 12 — AVOIDING GENERIC AI LANGUAGE (30.11)

\[9:54-10:49\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 12 / 18\. Claim, serif: Audiences recognise the tells on sight — and they cost you the trust you are building. Structure: an evidence wall — the business's own banned list filling from real drafts: delve · unlock · elevate · game-changer · rule-of-three lists · symmetrical sentences · the grand summary ending, each landing as a documented item with the standing-constraint line beneath. Evidence: the running-banned-list rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.11. Consequence, accent: Keep the list, feed it forward — it becomes part of your AI operating system.  
Purpose of this slide: Turn the AI tells into a standing constraint (30.11).  
Say:  
"Certain words, phrases and structural habits have become so strongly associated with AI-generated writing that audiences recognise them on sight. That recognition undermines exactly the authenticity a small business depends on.  
The usual tells: words like 'delve', 'unlock', 'elevate' and 'game-changer'; rule-of-three lists; overly symmetrical sentences; and a habit of ending pieces with a grand summary sentence that restates everything just said.  
Keep a running, business-specific list of these habits, built from your own drafts, and feed it back into future prompts as a standing constraint. The goal is not to hide that a tool was used. It is to make the final piece sound like a specific person with a point of view."  
Cue: The list is built from the room's own drafts, not from a generic list — say so before it is read.

### SLIDE 13 — AI-ASSISTED BRAINSTORMING (30.12)

\[10:49-11:45\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 13 / 18\. Claim, serif: Volume is the gift; curation is the job. Structure: a scorecard — a wide field of generated options as rows against two marked columns: worth developing and discard, most rows struck out, with the boundary that produced a usable list named across the top: a specific topic · a specific audience · a stated number · a length limit. Evidence: the boundary-beats-freedom rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.12. Consequence, accent: Ask for a bounded volume, then choose yourself.  
Purpose of this slide: Use volume with a boundary and a human filter (30.12).  
Say:  
"One of the most useful applications is generating raw ideas in volume, to be filtered afterwards by judgment: twenty content angles on one topic, ten hooks for the same video, several ways to frame a client story.  
The value is not that every idea is good — most will not be. It is that volume and speed make the handful worth developing easier to find.  
It works best with a clear boundary rather than complete freedom. 'Give me ideas' produces scattered output. 'Give me fifteen hooks for a video about this topic, aimed at this audience, each under fifteen words' produces a working list — and you still end it by selecting and rejecting, using judgment the model lacks."  
Cue: Most rows fail; the struck-out ones are the point, because curation is the work.

### SLIDE 14 — AI-ASSISTED SCRIPTING (30.13)

\[11:45-12:42\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 14 / 18\. Claim, serif: A script is not finished until it has been read aloud. Structure: a pipeline — four stages from what you already know to what you actually say: your talking points · a drafted structure or opening · a rough full pass · the read-aloud pass that restores your voice, the last stage lit as the one that decides whether it survives contact with the camera. Evidence: the read-aloud rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.13. Consequence, accent: Generate from your own points — then say it out loud before you record.  
Purpose of this slide: Place the read-aloud pass as the final scripting step (30.13).  
Say:  
"AI can accelerate scripting: outlining a structure, drafting an opening hook, or producing a rough pass at a full script from your talking points — particularly useful if you know what you want to say but struggle with the blank page.  
Quality depends on what you provide: the topic, the audience, the platform's length and pacing conventions, and an outline of the points you want to hit. A script generated from a vague topic needs far more rework than one from real talking points.  
And read the finished script aloud before you call it final: scripts that look fine on the page can be awkward to say, and the model cannot know how a sentence will feel in your mouth."  
Cue: The lit stage is the last one; do not let the room treat the draft as the deliverable.

### SLIDE 15 — AI-ASSISTED REPURPOSING (30.14)

\[12:42-13:39\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 15 / 18\. Claim, serif: Its job is to reshape what exists — not to invent what does not. Structure: a scorecard — one original piece as a row against the platforms it can become, each marked column naming that platform's conventions, length limit and audience expectation, with an added claims column left deliberately struck out. Evidence: the transformation-not-creation rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.14. Consequence, accent: Hand it the source in full, then hold it to reshaping.  
Purpose of this slide: Apply the source-material rule to repurposing (30.14).  
Say:  
"Repurposing is one of the strongest use cases, because the source exists and the task is transformation rather than creation. A long-form video becomes a set of short clips with suggested captions; a blog post becomes a thread of social posts; a client testimonial is reshaped for several platforms — all from the same original source.  
Give the model the original in full, along with the target platform's conventions, length limits and audience expectations. Its job is to reshape what exists, not to invent — evaluate it against that standard rather than asking it to add claims that were not in the source.  
Here the efficiency gains become most visible: one piece of material becoming five or six platform-specific pieces."  
Cue: The struck-out column is the discipline; reshaping is the task and invention is the failure.

### SLIDE 16 — BUILDING REUSABLE PROMPT SYSTEMS (30.15)

\[13:39-14:31\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 16 / 18\. Claim, serif: Capture the prompt once, and every future version starts ahead. Structure: a ladder / stack — three rungs of compounding investment: the first attempt, which takes several rounds · the learning captured into a standing template · the library of templates that becomes an operational asset, the top rung lit as the one transferable to a colleague. Evidence: the compounding-investment rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30 §30.15. Consequence, accent: Save the template; stop rebuilding it from memory.  
Purpose of this slide: Close the teaching on the reusable template (30.15).  
Say:  
"Successful prompts should be captured and reused rather than reinvented. A reusable prompt system is a saved, refined template for a recurring task — a weekly social post, a client update email, a video script outline — with your voice guidance, standing constraints and format requirements built in.  
Building these compounds. The first time may take several rounds to get right, and each round reveals something specific: a phrase to include, a phrase to avoid, a structure that lands.  
Over time you build a small internal library covering your most repeated needs — a documented version of how your business uses AI, transferable to a colleague rather than rebuilt from memory."  
Cue: The top rung is the section's argument: the library is an asset, not a note.

### SLIDE 17 — THE STUDENT AI WORKFLOW EXERCISE

\[14:31-15:21\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 17 / 18\. Claim, serif: One recurring task, one standing prompt, written by you. Structure: a workshop frame — the instruction on screen: choose one recurring piece · write the standing prompt — task, audience, format, avoid, voice, checks · run it once · keep the template, with tonight's refinement named beneath. Evidence: the finished template as the exercise's deliverable, sourced From your own workflow, started live and refined tonight. Consequence, accent: What the draft gets wrong is what tonight is for.  
Purpose of this slide: Author the Student AI Workflow Exercise (30.16) as a spoken instruction, with the template refined as homework.  
Say:  
"Now build the first entry in that library yourself. This is the last live work of Day 4, and it is the one that makes everything else in the Day repeatable.  
In the next five minutes: take one recurring piece of content you produce — a weekly post, a client update, a video outline. Write the standing prompt for it: the task, the audience, the format, what to avoid, your voice guidance, and any facts that must be checked. Then run it once and see what comes back.  
Keep that template. Tonight, refine it from what the draft got wrong, and bring it to Day 5."  
Cue: Five minutes, visible, and it completes the Day's four exercises. The template is the deliverable, not the post.

### SLIDE 18 — CLOSE OF CHAPTER 30 AND DAY 4

\[15:21-16:18\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 4 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 18 / 18\. Claim, serif: Amplified judgment or generic output — the direction depends on how you work with it. Structure: a comparison ledger — used with direction against used passively, matched on what each produces: higher output, faster and still in your voice on one side; material that could have come from any business on the other. Evidence: the no-memory-no-stake rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 30, close. Consequence, accent: Tomorrow: the rhythm that runs all of it.  
Purpose of this slide: Close the chapter on the collaborator, and close Day 4 into Day 5\.  
Say:  
"That is Day 4, and that is AI in practice. The tool is not the point; the method around it is.  
Treat these models as fast, capable collaborators with no memory of your business, no lived experience of your industry and no accountability for the final product. Given clear direction and a critical eye, they amplify your judgment and accelerate the work; used passively, they produce material that could have come from any business — because in a very real sense, it did.  
You are taking four things home from today: your repurposing map, your production workflow, your exported clip, and your prompt template. Tomorrow opens with those four, and turns them into a rhythm you can run on a schedule."  
Cue: Close the Day, not the chapter: hand to Day 5 and name the four pieces of work going home.

## CHAPTER 30 — VISUAL SPECIFICATION (TASK 2 — PHASE D INPUT)

Status: nothing here is built. Section 8 puts visuals after the script is approved and after the Step A look gate. It is written to CAMERA\_V2/VISUALS/SLIDE-ARCHITECTURE.md, the executive-density standard, so every slide is specified in the five layers with the component named from that standard's library, an evidence element with its provenance, and a consequence line the room can act on.  
The demonstration rule, applied to a chapter about a working method. The subject is a loop, not a list, so the deck is built on input against output with the loop between them: what goes into the tool on one side, what comes back on the other, and the revision that closes the gap. Every instrument shows a real input changing a real output — a vague request and a briefed one, an unconstrained draft and its editing cost, a described voice and a shown one — because the chapter's whole claim is that the input decides the output, and a claim about causation has to be drawn as a change.  
Build-stage sizes. One self-contained HTML file per chapter, 1920 × 1080 stage that scales, no internet, system fonts, three colours with the one accent, serif claim, sans elsewhere, no label under 32 px, lines at least 3 px, 8% safe margin, reduced-motion shows every layer in its final state.  
Slide 01 — The LLM Chapter Opens. Type: six-rung working method. Build: 2 steps. Component: ladder / stack — the chapter's method in six rungs. Layers: chrome; claim, The tool is not the point. The method around it is.; the six rungs; the lit final rung; the consequence line. What changes: the first five rungs lay down in order; the second step lights the capture-the-template rung and brings up the consequence line. Why: the chapter is a sequence, and a ladder whose last rung is the one that makes the others repeatable is the sequence's whole argument.  
Slide 02 — What an LLM Actually Does. Type: does-against-does-not comparison. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger — what it does against what it does not do, matched on the same system. Layers: chrome; claim, It predicts the next plausible word — it does not know, and it does not think.; the two columns; the no-alarm row; the consequence line. What changes: the capability column fills with fluent, well-organised output; the limit column fills with knowing, thinking and raising an alarm; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's fact is the foundation of the chapter, and two matched columns stop the room hearing only the useful half.  
Slide 03 — Context. Type: context ladder. Build: 3 steps. Component: ladder / stack — five rungs from a vague request to a fully specified one, with output quality climbing. Layers: chrome; claim, The single biggest lever you hold — and the one most people never pull.; the five rungs; the climbing quality marker; the consequence line. What changes: the vague request sits alone and produces a flat generic block; the rungs are added and the output block changes shape toward the specific; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's claim is that one lever moves everything, and a visible change in the same output as the rungs climb is that lever drawn.  
Slide 04 — Prompting. Type: vague-against-briefed ledger. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger — a vague ask against a briefed ask, matched on the four rows: task, audience, format, what to avoid. Layers: chrome; claim, A prompt is a brief — and a brief has four parts.; the two columns; the four rows; the consequence line. What changes: the ask column holds one flat line and four empty rows; the brief column fills all four rows; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the section gives four named parts, and four rows that one column never fills is what makes the gap in output understandable.  
Slide 05 — Providing Source Material. Type: source-folder wall. Build: 3 steps. Component: evidence wall — what a business already owns landing into the folder, empty cells visible. Layers: chrome; claim, Real material beats a good description of the material, every time.; the folder's cells; the five named items with their provenance; the consequence line. What changes: the empty cells sit visible first; the items land one per pass — transcript, notes, past post, review, competitor post; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's recommendation is a habit of keeping material ready, and a wall with cells still empty is exactly the state the habit fixes.  
Slide 06 — Giving the AI a Job. Type: whose-eyes decision bench. Build: 2 steps. Component: decision bench — a draft held centrally with a read-it-as-yourself exit and a read-it-as-a-named-role exit. Layers: chrome; claim, Give it a role, and it reviews your work through eyes that are not yours.; the bench and its two exits; each lens's catch and blind spot; the consequence line. What changes: the as-yourself exit lights first with its blind spot; the second step lights the named-role exit with what it catches and brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's value is a perspective that differs from the owner's, and a bench with two lenses is the only honest way to show that.  
Slide 07 — Giving the AI Constraints. Type: constrained-against-unconstrained cost ledger. Build: 3 steps. Component: cost ledger — the same piece run twice, with the unconstrained draft's editing cost accumulating per section. Layers: chrome; claim, Constraints are not a limit on creativity. They are what makes the output usable.; the line items; the running totals; the consequence line. What changes: the unconstrained column's editing hours accumulate; the constrained column runs the same list to a lower total; the third step marks the difference and brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's argument is cost, and a total that only diverges as it climbs is what a ledger is for.  
Slide 08 — Iteration. Type: three-cycle revision timeline. Build: 3 steps. Component: timeline with milestones — the draft's three cycles on one rule, cost per cycle falling. Layers: chrome; claim, Specific feedback, not a new prompt, is what closes the gap.; the three markers; the feedback line at each; the consequence line. What changes: the first response lands with a vague 'make it better' that changes little; the second marker carries the targeted instruction and a real revision; the third step lands the usable draft and brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's claim is that specificity is what moves the draft, and a timeline where only the specific cycle changes the work shows it.  
Slide 09 — Criticism and Revision. Type: critic's-gate flow. Build: 3 steps. Component: gate / flow — a draft arriving at a critic's gate by either a review-this request or an ask-for-weaknesses request. Layers: chrome; claim, Ask for praise and you get praise. Ask for the weaknesses, and it earns its keep.; the gate and its two requests; the safe-approval tag; the consequence line. What changes: the review-this request passes and returns a generic approval; the same draft returns through the weaknesses request with three named faults; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's technique only works when the prompt leaves no safe answer, and a gate that returns approval by default is that risk drawn.  
Slide 10 — Fact Checking. Type: verification gate over every specific. Build: 3 steps. Component: gate / flow — a specific claim arriving at a verification gate with a confirmed exit and a published-anyway exit. Layers: chrome; claim, Nothing in the output tells you whether it is true.; the gate and its two exits; the five miss categories; the consequence line. What changes: the claim publishes first with its category tags lit against it; the claim returns and passes verification; the third step sets the gate as the last step of every draft and brings up the consequence line. Why: Chapter 29 already drew this gate for research, and re-drawing it here as the final step of any draft is what makes it a habit rather than a stage.  
Slide 11 — Maintaining Personal Voice. Type: described-against-shown voice ledger. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger — describing the voice against showing the voice, matched on what the model can imitate. Layers: chrome; claim, Show it three paragraphs of your voice — do not describe the voice.; the two columns; the imitation row; the consequence line. What changes: the description column fills with adjectives and the imitation row stays weak; the shown column fills with three real paragraphs and the row strengthens; the third step brings up the consequence line and adds the reader's own pass. Why: the section is explicitly about showing over describing, and a row that only strengthens on real samples is that instruction made visible.  
Slide 12 — Avoiding Generic AI Language. Type: banned-tells wall. Build: 3 steps. Component: evidence wall — the business's own list of tells landing from real drafts, with the standing-constraint line beneath. Layers: chrome; claim, Audiences recognise the tells on sight — and they cost you the trust you are building.; the list cells; the seven named tells; the consequence line. What changes: the list fills one per pass from real drafts; the standing-constraint line attaches beneath it; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's recommendation is a running, business-specific list fed forward, and a wall built from the room's own drafts is the difference between a list and a habit.  
Slide 13 — AI-Assisted Brainstorming. Type: bounded-volume scorecard. Build: 3 steps. Component: scorecard — generated options as rows against worth developing and discard, with the boundary that produced the list named across the top. Layers: chrome; claim, Volume is the gift; curation is the job.; the option rows; the two marked columns with the failures struck out; the consequence line. What changes: the options land in volume; the columns are marked and most rows are struck out; the third step brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's method is a bounded ask plus human curation, and most rows failing is what makes the curation the work.  
Slide 14 — AI-Assisted Scripting. Type: talking-points-to-read-aloud pipeline. Build: 3 steps. Component: pipeline — four stages from what you know to what you say, the last lit. Layers: chrome; claim, A script is not finished until it has been read aloud.; the four stages; the lit read-aloud stage; the consequence line. What changes: talking points and the drafted structure land; the rough full pass follows; the third step lights the read-aloud pass as the stage that decides and brings up the consequence line. Why: the section's final instruction is the one people skip, and a pipeline whose last stage is lit is how a skipped stage is shown to matter.  
Slide 15 — AI-Assisted Repurposing. Type: transformation scorecard. Build: 3 steps. Layers: chrome; claim, Its job is to reshape what exists — not to invent what does not.; the source row; the platform columns with their conventions; the consequence line. Why: the section's standard is reshaping rather than inventing, and a column deliberately struck out is that standard enforced on the slide.

## 7\. What this Day proves about the budget method

| Day | Words | vs 10,500 | Live | vs 120:00 | Chapters over their allowance | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | 10,633 | \+133 (1:04 over) | 121:04 | 1:04 over | 4 of 5 | FAIL, accepted as an exception |
| 2 | 10,484 | −16 (8 seconds under) | 119:51 | 9 seconds inside | 3 of 7 | PASS |
| 3 | 10,088 | −412 (3:18 under) | 116:42 | 3:18 inside | 0 of 5 | PASS |
| 4 | 10,478 | −22 (11 seconds under) | 119:49 | 11 seconds inside | 1 of 6 | PASS |

Read down the "Chapters over" column and the mechanism is plain. Day 1 cut each chapter to its own allowance and accepted all four overs, which summed to a breach. Day 2 wrote the last four deliberately under theirs, netting −16. Day 3 spent none of its tolerance at all and banked 3:18. Day 4 sits between them: it spent 13 words of tolerance on its final chapter and still landed under, because the chapter was written to the words the Day actually had left rather than to the ceiling it was entitled to. That is the second application of the Day-2 lesson (its Chapter 13\) and it is what a Day with six chapters and a 2,025-word last allowance has to do. Section 2's limits are unchanged, Day 1's exception stays an exception, and Day 4 does not lean on it.  
One thing Day 4 shows that Day 3 did not. Day 3's clearance came from its chapters being written well under their allowances (−187 on Chapter 15, −113 on Chapter 16). Day 4's came from arithmetic performed at the end of the Day: five chapters landed within 11 words of their allowances, and the whole margin came from the decision to write Chapter 30 to 2,060 instead of 2,085. Both work; the second one only works if the writer knows the Day's remaining budget before writing the last chapter.

## CHAPTER 31 — AVOIDING THE AI TOOL TRAP

### SLIDE 01 — THE TOOL TRAP OPENS

\[0:00-0:52\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 01 / 12\. Claim, serif: The fastest way to lose money on AI is not to buy the wrong tool. It is to buy ten of them. Structure: a fan-out — one card labelled one problem, one tool splitting into a row of ten subscription cards beneath it, each carrying the same small monthly figure beneath it, the row's total count climbing. Evidence: the ten-subscription pattern sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31, opening. Consequence, accent: Every tool has to earn its line. That is this chapter.  
Purpose of this slide: Open the chapter's territory and name the pattern it exists to prevent (§31.1 setup).  
Say:  
"You have spent four days learning to make content well: the voice, the camera, the light, the sound, the edit, and the way AI accelerates all of it. Today the subject is the bill underneath.  
There is a pattern that costs small operations more than almost anything else, and this chapter names it: the ten-subscription problem. One tool for writing, one for images, one for video, one for scheduling, one for transcription — most barely opened, every one billed monthly whether it is used or not.  
The trap is not one bad decision. It is ten reasonable ones. And the fix is a filter you will use from here."  
Cue: The climbing count is the whole argument; do not read the ten labels out — let the row accumulate.

### SLIDE 02 — THE TEN-SUBSCRIPTION PROBLEM (31.1)

\[0:52-1:43\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 02 / 12\. Claim, serif: Each addition felt reasonable. The stack did not. Structure: a cost ledger — ten monthly lines, one per tool, each marked with the month it was added, and a total line beneath showing what the stack costs against what the content work returns. Evidence: the gradual-accumulation rule and the never-cancelled-the-first pattern sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.1. Consequence, accent: Treat every subscription as a reviewed decision, not an add-on.  
Purpose of this slide: Define the pattern and price it honestly (§31.1).  
Say:  
"The trap forms gradually. A new tool solves one specific problem well, so it gets added. Weeks later a different tool promises to solve a different problem slightly better, so it gets added too — often without cancelling the first, which is how a stack ends up with two tools doing one job.  
Each decision looks fine on its own. The cumulative effect is overlapping subscriptions costing more per month than the content work returns, especially for a business still finding its footing.  
So the fix is not to avoid paid tools — some genuinely earn their cost. It is to treat each one as a deliberate, reviewed decision."  
Cue: The total line is the moment; let it sit before the consequence.

### SLIDE 03 — TOOLS VS. WORKFLOW (31.2)

\[1:43-2:39\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 03 / 12\. Claim, serif: You can own powerful tools and still have no workflow. Structure: a comparison ledger — a tool (one piece of software doing one job) against a workflow (the real sequence from idea to published piece), matched on what each actually gets done, with the workflow column showing the unglamorous steps no single tool covers. Evidence: the workflow-first rule and the shop-for-tools mistake sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.2. Consequence, accent: Map the steps first, then buy for the bottleneck.  
Purpose of this slide: Separate the two ideas and reorder the decision (§31.2).  
Say:  
"A tool is one piece of software doing one job. A workflow is the sequence of steps, decisions and tools you actually use to get from an idea to something published. You can own an impressive collection of powerful tools and have no working workflow at all.  
The common mistake is to shop for tools before the workflow exists, which buys capability you do not yet know how to use. Do it in the other order: map the steps content actually goes through — idea, draft, review, publish — then ask which step is genuinely slowed down by a missing capability.  
Speeding up a step that was never the bottleneck is worth nothing, however well the tool performs."  
Cue: The unglamorous-steps column is the point; the wrong order is the mistake to name.

### SLIDE 04 — FREE TOOLS FIRST (31.3)

\[2:39-3:31\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 04 / 12\. Claim, serif: The free tier is not a trial. It is the default. Structure: a ladder / stack — the order of adoption as rungs: free tier, used in real production · the actual limit felt, not anticipated · the upgrade, earned, each rung labelled with what has to be true before the next. Evidence: the free-tier-ceilings rule (volume, resolution, speed and the top model limited rather than functionality blocked) sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.3. Consequence, accent: Upgrade when the limit is felt. Never when it is imagined.  
Purpose of this slide: Install free-first as the standing default (§31.3).  
Say:  
"For nearly every task this course covers — writing, images, transcription, editing — a capable free tier exists, and it is sufficient for a business just building its content operation. So start free, use it in real production long enough to understand its limits, and upgrade only once those limits are felt rather than anticipated.  
Free tiers usually limit volume, resolution, speed, or access to the most capable model. They rarely block the core function — so a free tier is normally enough to prove a workflow and publish real content before the revenue justifies paying.  
It costs a little patience and buys discipline: every upgrade has to earn its way in."  
Cue: The felt-versus-imagined line is the rule; keep the ladder visible as you say it.

### SLIDE 05 — WHEN A PAID TOOL IS JUSTIFIED (31.4)

\[3:31-4:26\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 05 / 12\. Claim, serif: A real bottleneck, and a use that will recur. Both, not either. Structure: a gate / flow — a proposed upgrade entering two gates in sequence, the first labelled does it remove a bottleneck that costs more than the tool? and the second will it be used constantly, week after week?, with the exits marked wait and adopt. Evidence: the two-test justification rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.4. Consequence, accent: Name the task it fixes, and the monthly cost of not fixing it.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the concrete test that a subscription has to pass (§31.4).  
Say:  
"A paid tool is justified when it removes a real, recurring bottleneck that currently costs more than the subscription would. That is a concrete test, not a feeling: before upgrading, name the specific task that is slow, painful or impossible on the free tier, and estimate what that costs each month.  
The second test is repetition. A capability used constantly, week after week, justifies a recurring cost far more easily than one that might be useful once. For a one-time need, a single purchase or a free trial beats a standing subscription.  
When both tests are met, the tool has earned its place. When only one is, or neither, the answer is usually to wait."  
Cue: Both gates, not either: if the second gate is skipped, the subscription returns later as waste.

### SLIDE 06 — SUBSCRIPTIONS (31.5)

\[4:26-5:18\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 06 / 12\. Claim, serif: A subscription does not ask to be re-justified. You have to build the moment yourself. Structure: a decision bench — a fixed monthly review held centrally, with one question on it: was this used for real client or content work this month?, and two exits: cancel and keep, with an annual-plan check beneath. Evidence: the monthly-review rule and the annual-billing caution sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.5. Consequence, accent: Untouched this month is the strongest reason to cancel.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the recurring habit that stops the stack from drifting (§31.5).  
Say:  
"A subscription bills automatically whether the tool is used or not. That is convenient for planning and dangerous for a small operation, because the cost keeps recurring long after the reason for it has faded.  
So put a subscription review on a fixed schedule — the start of every month, say — and check every active subscription against one question: was this used for real client or content work in the past month? If it was not touched, cancel it.  
Do the annual-plan arithmetic at the same review. A year up front costs less but locks the commitment in, so it belongs only on tools that have passed the justification test."  
Cue: The single question is the instrument; keep the review fixed and short.

### SLIDE 07 — CREDITS AND TOKENS (31.6)

\[5:18-6:16\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 07 / 12\. Claim, serif: Credits make cost invisible one use at a time. Structure: an annotated chart — one finished image or clip drawn as a bar, with the regenerated attempts, revisions and experiments stacked inside it, each marked with its credit cost, so the bar's true height is only visible at the end. Evidence: the cost-per-output rule and the consumption-versus-subscription comparison sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.6. Consequence, accent: Track cost per finished piece, not cost per credit.  
Purpose of this slide: Handle consumption billing and its particular blind spot (§31.6).  
Say:  
"Some AI tools, especially for images and video, bill by consumption rather than a flat monthly fee: a pool of credits spent each use, which runs out and has to be topped up. That can be cheaper for occasional work — nothing sits idle in a slow month — but it needs a different kind of attention.  
The risk is losing track of the real cost per output. One project can quietly consume credits across regenerated attempts, revisions and experiments, and because each use feels small, the total is easy to lose.  
So track cost per finished piece of content, not cost per credit. And before committing to a credit tool for regular work, compare a typical month against a flat subscription."  
Cue: The stacked bar is the blind spot made visible; end on the per-finished-piece rule.

### SLIDE 08 — MODEL SELECTION (31.7)

\[6:16-7:10\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 08 / 12\. Claim, serif: Most people leave the model on whatever it defaulted to. That is a cost decision made by nobody. Structure: a comparison ledger — routine, low-stakes tasks against tasks needing judgment or a final draft, matched on what each actually needs, with the default setting shown sitting on one side regardless. Evidence: the match-the-model-to-the-task rule and both failure modes (over-defaulting to the expensive model, under-defaulting to the cheapest) sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.7. Consequence, accent: Match the model to the task, then change it back.  
Purpose of this slide: Turn model choice into a deliberate lever (§31.7).  
Say:  
"Most AI platforms now offer a choice between underlying models — usually a faster, cheaper one and a more capable, more expensive one. It is a genuine cost and quality lever, and it is routinely ignored: whatever is selected by default gets used for everything.  
The working principle is to match capability to difficulty. Routine work — a quick draft, a simple rewrite — rarely needs the most powerful model available. Nuanced judgment about your specific situation, or a final draft, is where the capable model earns its cost.  
Both defaults fail. The expensive model on everything inflates cost with no gain on everyday work. The cheapest on demanding work produces output that needs more correction."  
Cue: The two failure modes are why this is a lever and not a preference; keep both.

### SLIDE 09 — AVOIDING TOOL CHASING (31.8)

\[7:10-8:04\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 09 / 12\. Claim, serif: A new tool is not a reason to adopt a new tool. Structure: a decision bench — a new release held centrally, with two exits named in the tool's own language: it is new and impressive and it closes a gap I currently feel, the first exit labelled with what it costs in learning time and integration, the second with the workflow it repairs. Evidence: the concrete-felt-problem rule and the wide-but-shallow stack sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.8. Consequence, accent: A healthy stack changes slowly and deliberately.  
Purpose of this slide: Name the habit and give it a cost (§31.8).  
Say:  
"Tool chasing is the habit of adopting the newest AI tool because the next release might finally make everything easier — rather than because of a concrete gap in the workflow you already run. It is seductive in a field that ships impressive releases constantly.  
The cost is not only financial. Every tool adopted takes time to learn and integrate. Someone constantly switching rarely goes deep enough to use any of them well, and ends up with a stack that is wide but shallow — many capabilities half-learned, none mastered.  
So the rule is the one from earlier: a new tool earns adoption when it solves a concrete problem in the workflow you already run."  
Cue: Learning time is the invisible price; say it before the consequence lands.

### SLIDE 10 — BUILDING A SMALL AI STACK (31.9)

\[8:04-9:00\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 10 / 12\. Claim, serif: For coverage, not collection. Structure: a fan-out — the workflow's recurring steps as the source, with four exits and no more: one primary language model · one image or video tool · one or two utilities for transcription or scheduling, each labelled with the step it serves and each checked for overlap with the others. Evidence: the handful-of-tools rule and the already-known-tool preference sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.9. Consequence, accent: Before adding anything, ask whether what you own already does it.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the shape a finished stack should have (§31.9).  
Say:  
"A small AI stack is a deliberately limited set of tools with clear, distinct jobs that together cover the real needs of your workflow. For most solo operations that is honestly a handful: one language model, one image or video tool, and one utility for transcription or scheduling.  
Build it for coverage, not collection. Every tool should map to a recurring step in the workflow you run — and before adding anything, ask whether something you already own could do the job. A tool you already know and use usually beats a marginally better one that means starting over.  
Revisit the stack on the same schedule as your subscriptions, but review it to consolidate, not to replace."  
Cue: Four exits and no more is the shape; the overlap check is the working habit.

### SLIDE 11 — EVALUATING NEW AI TOOLS (31.10)

\[9:00-9:54\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 11 / 12\. Claim, serif: Four questions, in order. Fail one and it waits. Structure: a gate / flow — a candidate tool entering four gates in sequence: a real gap in the workflow today · can I test it before paying? · does the cost comparison hold? · does it fit my stack cleanly?, with a single exit adopt reached only through all four. Evidence: the four-question filter and the overlap-as-a-sign rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31 §31.10. Consequence, accent: A tool that fails one question is set aside, not deleted.  
Purpose of this slide: Give the standing filter and close the chapter's argument (§31.10).  
Say:  
"When a genuinely new tool appears worth considering, run it through a short, consistent evaluation rather than adopting on impulse. Four questions, in order.  
One: does it address a real gap in the workflow you run today, not a hypothetical future need? Two: is there a free tier or trial to test that use before any payment is committed? Three: is the bottleneck it solves costing more than the tool would? Four: does it fit the stack — will it replace something you use, or sit alongside it with meaningful overlap, which usually means it is not needed?  
Only a tool clearing all four is adopted. One that fails any of them waits."  
Cue: Four gates in order; the set-aside ending matters as much as the adoption.

### SLIDE 12 — CLOSE OF CHAPTER 31

\[9:54-10:47\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · A: AI ACCELERATION · 12 / 12\. Claim, serif: A stack you can name is a stack you can defend. Structure: a ladder / stack — the chapter restacked as one recurring loop: map the workflow · start free · justify on a felt bottleneck · review monthly · match the model to the task · filter every new tool, the six rungs marked as one repeating discipline rather than a one-time clear-out. Evidence: the anti-trap line closing the chapter sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 31, close. Consequence, accent: Next: the content format that has to work in sixty seconds.  
Purpose of this slide: Close the chapter on the recurring discipline and hand to Chapter 33 within the same Day.  
Say:  
"That is the tool trap, and the way out is not frugality for its own sake. Map the workflow before you shop. Start on free tiers and pay when a limit is felt. Match the model to the task. Review every subscription monthly. Treat a new tool as something that must close a gap you can point at.  
Do that and the stack you end up with is small enough to know properly, every tool in it earning its line.  
Money saved is only half of it. The other half is attention: a stack you understand lets the craft run. Next: the format that has to work in sixty seconds."  
Cue: Hand to Chapter 33, not to a break: Day 5 continues here.

## CHAPTER 31 — VISUAL SPECIFICATION (TASK 2 — PHASE D INPUT)

Status: nothing here is built. Section 8 puts visuals after the script is approved and after the Step A look gate. Day 1's five files and Days 2, 3 and 4's twelve carry this same section in this same shape, against the same standard and the same vocabulary; this is that section written for a new chapter rather than a revision of an old one. It is written to CAMERA\_V2/VISUALS/SLIDE-ARCHITECTURE.md, the executive-density standard, so every slide is specified in the five layers with the component named from that standard's library, an evidence element with its provenance, and a consequence line the room can act on.  
The demonstration rule, applied to a chapter about spending. The subject is discipline, and discipline in the abstract is invisible, so every instrument here is a decision with a price on both sides — a cost ledger, a matched comparison, a gate, or a bench. Nothing tells the room to be careful with money; every slide stages the alternative and lets the room see what each one costs.  
Build-stage sizes. One self-contained HTML file per chapter, 1920 × 1080 stage that scales, no internet, system fonts, three colours with the one accent, serif claim, sans elsewhere, no label under 32 px, lines at least 3 px, 8% safe margin, reduced-motion shows every layer in its final state. Build steps: 30 across the twelve slides, plus 1 for the supplementary board — 31 in total, and the deliverable index below sums to the same 31\.  
Slide 01 — The Tool Trap Opens. Type: one-to-many subscription fan-out. Build: 2 steps. Component: fan-out — one source card splitting into a row of ten subscription cards with a climbing count. Layers: chrome; claim, The fastest way to lose money on AI is not to buy the wrong tool. It is to buy ten of them.; the source card and the ten-card row; the running total; the consequence line. What changes: the single card lands alone and bills once; the second step fans it into the row and the count climbs past the point of sense. Why: the chapter's whole claim is accumulation, and a single honest card becoming ten is that claim drawn rather than asserted.  
Slide 02 — The Ten-Subscription Problem. Type: ten-line cost ledger. Build: 3 steps. Component: cost ledger — one monthly line per tool with the month it was added, and a total beneath. Layers: chrome; claim, Each addition felt reasonable. The stack did not.; the ten monthly lines arriving in date order; the total line set against what the content work returns; the consequence line. What changes: the lines add one per step, each looking small; the third step brings up the total and the comparison, which is the first moment the stack is visible as one number. Why: the trap is a sum nobody ever looked at, and only a total line makes accumulation legible.  
Slide 03 — Tools vs. Workflow. Type: tool-against-workflow comparison. Build: 2 steps. Component: comparison ledger — a tool against a workflow, matched on what each actually gets done. Layers: chrome; claim, You can own powerful tools and still have no workflow.; the two columns; the unglamorous workflow steps no single tool covers; the consequence line. What changes: both columns fill and the tool column glows first; the second step completes the workflow column — idea, draft, review, repurpose, publish, measure — and brings up the consequence line that reorders the decision. Why: the section's argument is sequence, and a completed column beside a bright but idle one is the honest picture of buying capability before process.  
Slide 04 — Free Tools First. Type: four-rung adoption ladder. Build: 3 steps. Component: ladder / stack — free tier used in real production, the felt limit, the earned upgrade. Layers: chrome; claim, The free tier is not a trial. It is the default.; the rungs; each rung's entry condition; the consequence line. What changes: the free rung lands with its condition; the second step lights the felt-versus-anticipated distinction at the rung's edge; the third reaches the upgrade rung and brings up the consequence. Why: the rule is an order of operations, and an order is only visible as steps with conditions between them.  
Slide 05 — When a Paid Tool Is Justified. Type: two-gate justification flow. Build: 3 steps. Component: gate / flow — a proposed upgrade passing a bottleneck gate then a repetition gate, with wait and adopt exits. Layers: chrome; claim, A real bottleneck, and a use that will recur. Both, not either.; the two gates in sequence; the exits marked wait and adopt; the consequence line. What changes: the upgrade reaches the first gate and the wait exit lights; the second step opens the repetition gate and lights the adopt exit; the third names the price of the bottleneck before the consequence. Why: the test is conjunctive, and a flow that can only reach adopt through both gates shows that better than a sentence of prose.  
Slide 06 — Subscriptions. Type: fixed-monthly-review decision bench. Build: 2 steps. Component: decision bench — one question held centrally with cancel and keep exits, and an annual-plan check beneath. Layers: chrome; claim, A subscription does not ask to be re-justified. You have to build the moment yourself.; the single question; the two exits; the annual check and the consequence line. What changes: the question lands with the calendar mark beside it; the second step works one subscription through both exits and brings up the annual-billing caution and the consequence. Why: the section's device is a habit, and a habit needs a fixed moment on screen before it needs an argument.  
Slide 07 — Credits and Tokens. Type: cost-per-output stacked bar. Build: 3 steps. Component: annotated chart — one finished piece as a bar with the attempts, revisions and experiments stacked inside it and priced. Layers: chrome; claim, Credits make cost invisible one use at a time.; the finished-piece bar; the stacked internal cost, each segment priced; the consequence line. What changes: the bar starts as one clean output; the second step stacks the regenerated attempts and revisions inside it; the third totals the stack and brings up the per-finished-piece rule. Why: consumption billing hides its total inside many small uses, and only a stacked bar shows the height one credit purchase at a time never reveals.  
Slide 08 — Model Selection. Type: routine-against-demanding comparison. Build: 2 steps. Component: comparison ledger — routine tasks against judgment tasks, matched on what each needs, with the default setting parked on one side. Layers: chrome; claim, Most people leave the model on whatever it defaulted to. That is a cost decision made by nobody.; the two columns; the parked default; the two failure modes and the consequence line. What changes: the columns match on their work; the second step moves the default off its park and lights both failure modes — expensive model on routine work, cheap model on demanding work — before the consequence. Why: the section's lever is a switch nobody flips, and a switch that has to move is more convincing than an instruction to move it.  
Slide 09 — Avoiding Tool Chasing. Type: novelty-against-gap decision bench. Build: 2 steps. Component: decision bench — a new release held centrally, with a novelty exit and a felt-gap exit, the first carrying its learning and integration cost. Layers: chrome; claim, A new tool is not a reason to adopt a new tool.; the bench and its two exits; the learning-cost label; the consequence line. What changes: the novelty exit lights first with the hours it will cost to learn and integrate; the second step lights the felt-gap exit, which is the only one that repairs a workflow, then brings up the consequence. Why: chasing is a habit with a hidden price, and pricing the novelty exit is what makes the chapter's rule feel like arithmetic rather than restraint.  
Slide 10 — Building a Small AI Stack. Type: job-mapped stack fan-out. Build: 3 steps. Component: fan-out — the workflow's recurring steps feeding four exits and no more, each checking for overlap. Layers: chrome; claim, For coverage, not collection.; the four exits; the overlap check drawn between them; the consequence line. What changes: the four exits land one per step, each labelled with the step it serves; the third step draws the overlap check between them and brings up the ask-what-you-own rule. Why: the section defines a stack by what it covers, and a fan-out with a fixed number of exits held against an overlap check is that definition drawn.  
Slide 11 — Evaluating New AI Tools. Type: four-question gate sequence. Build: 3 steps. Component: gate / flow — a candidate tool passing four gates in order, with adopt reachable only through all four. Layers: chrome; claim, Four questions, in order. Fail one and it waits.; the four gates; the single adopt exit; the consequence line. What changes: the candidate clears the first two gates in one step; the third step holds it at the cost comparison and the fit check, and lights the set-aside exit as plainly as the adopt exit. Why: the filter's value is that it is finite and ordered, and a gate sequence that visibly stops a plausible tool is the chapter's whole argument paid off.  
Slide 12 — Close Of Chapter 31\. Type: six-rung discipline loop echoing Slide 04, resolved. Build: 2 steps. Component: ladder / stack — the chapter restacked as one repeating loop from workflow map to new-tool filter. Layers: chrome; claim, A stack you can name is a stack you can defend.; the six rungs; the recurrence mark that makes it a loop; the consequence line. What changes: the stack assembles base to top in one pass; the second step closes it into a cycle and brings up the consequence line pointing to the next chapter of the Day. Why: the close must gather a ten-part chapter into one orderable discipline and hand inside the same Day — the loop is both the recap and the hand-off.  
Supplementary — the four-question filter board (§31.10). Type: filter scorecard for the subsection that has no worksheet. Build: 1 step. Component: scorecard — the four questions as columns, a row per candidate tool, the set-aside and adopt marks at the end of each row. Layers: chrome and the board itself, with the business writing in; no consequence rule, because the board is an instrument rather than a slide. What changes: the business runs one candidate tool it is actually considering across the four columns. Why: §31.11's worksheet was dropped on John's ruling, and this is the smallest honest substitute — visible and named rather than quietly assumed.

## CHAPTER 33 — THE 60-SECOND AUTHORITY VIDEO

### SLIDE 01 — THE 60-SECOND FORMAT OPENS

\[0:00-0:24\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · CONTENT CREATION PRACTICALS · 01 / 12\. Claim, serif: Sixty seconds is not a shorter video. It is a different format. Structure: an annotated chart — a sixty-second bar divided into five unlabelled segments in proportion (hook · setup · teaching · proof · CTA), the teaching segment visibly the largest, the whole bar left uncoloured until the chapter lights it segment by segment. Evidence: the demonstrate-expertise-in-under-a-minute rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 33, opening. Consequence, accent: The proportions are the format. Everything else follows from them.  
Purpose of this slide: Open the chapter's territory and install the timeline the next five slides advance (§33.1 setup).  
Say:  
"The 60-second authority video is a repeatable format with one purpose: proving real expertise in under a minute to a specific audience.  
Because the format is short, the proportions do the work. Five segments share the minute: hook, setup, teaching, proof, ask.  
We will walk that bar, then record your own."  
Cue: The uncoloured bar is the promise; do not label the segments — the next five slides do it.

### SLIDE 02 — SELECTING THE TOPIC (33.1)

\[0:24-0:53\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · CONTENT CREATION PRACTICALS · 02 / 12\. Claim, serif: The best topic is already written down. You just have not recorded it yet. Structure: a decision bench — two topic sources held centrally: invented in the abstract and a real question a client asked, the second labelled with how it arrives and the first with what it costs in relevance. Evidence: the running-list rule and the no-room-to-recover rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 33 §33.1. Consequence, accent: Keep a running list of real questions. That list is the topic source.  
Purpose of this slide: Fix where topics come from and why breadth fails here (§33.1).  
Say:  
"Topic selection matters more here than anywhere else: sixty seconds cannot recover from a topic that is too broad.  
The strongest topics are narrow questions your audience really holds — something a prospect asked, or a mistake you see repeatedly. A real question beats one invented in the abstract.  
Keep a running list of them. That list is your topic source."  
Cue: The real-question source is the whole habit; land it before the consequence.

### SLIDE 03 — HOOK (33.2)

\[0:53-1:21\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · CONTENT CREATION PRACTICALS · 03 / 12\. Claim, serif: Three to five seconds, and the clock is already running. Structure: the 60-second bar with its first segment lit — the hook slice filled and labelled with its cost: a six-second start \= more than ten percent spent before the first point. Evidence: the name-the-misconception and confident-claim hook rules, and the draft-several-and-pick rule, sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 33 §33.2. Consequence, accent: Name the wrong belief, or state the claim. Do not warm up.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the hook's tighter constraint and its two working shapes (§33.2).  
Say:  
"The hook is the first three to five seconds, and the constraint is tighter here: a start that takes six or seven seconds has spent a tenth of the video.  
Two shapes work: name the misconception, stating the wrong belief before correcting it; or state your narrow topic as a confident claim.  
Draft a few and keep the strongest."  
Cue: The lit slice is the argument; the ten-percent line is what makes it painful.

### SLIDE 04 — SETUP (33.3)

\[1:21-1:49\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · CONTENT CREATION PRACTICALS · 04 / 12\. Claim, serif: Just enough context to make the point matter. Nothing more. Structure: the bar advanced — the setup slice lit beside the hook, capped at five to ten seconds, with two exits named: the cost of getting this wrong and who this is for. Evidence: the frame-the-stakes rule and the write-hook-and-setup-together rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 33 §33.3. Consequence, accent: Frame the stakes, then move.  
Purpose of this slide: Keep the bridge short and give it a job (§33.3).  
Say:  
"The setup is the bridge between hook and teaching: just enough context to show why this matters, without drifting into an introduction.  
It takes five to ten seconds and usually does one of two things — states the cost of getting this wrong, or who it is most for.  
Write hook and setup together, and check neither restates the other."  
Cue: Two exits, one purpose: never spend setup on background the audience already has.

### SLIDE 05 — TEACHING (33.4)

\[1:49-2:17\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · CONTENT CREATION PRACTICALS · 05 / 12\. Claim, serif: The teaching owns the middle — thirty to thirty-five of the sixty. Structure: the bar advanced — the teaching slice lit as by far the longest, with the removal test written across it: if cutting this sentence loses the point, it stays; if not, it goes. Evidence: the single-central-argument rule and the jargon-as-friction rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 33 §33.4. Consequence, accent: One argument, plain words, every sentence earning its place.  
Purpose of this slide: Make the teaching the majority of the runtime and give it its editing test (§33.4).  
Say:  
"The teaching takes the majority of the runtime — thirty to thirty-five seconds — delivering the answer the hook promised, built around one argument.  
Every sentence has to earn its place. Ask of each: if I cut this, do I lose the point? There is no room for hedging, or restating what has landed.  
Plain words only — friction costs watch time."  
Cue: The longest slice has to look the longest; the removal test is the working tool.

### SLIDE 06 — PROOF (33.5)

\[2:17-2:42\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · CONTENT CREATION PRACTICALS · 06 / 12\. Claim, serif: One specific detail beats a claim of experience. Structure: the bar advanced — the proof slice lit at five to ten seconds, holding a single sharp detail, with a second, greyed slice beside it marked a general claim of expertise left unlit. Evidence: the proof-reinforces-the-teaching-point rule and the specific-detail rule sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 33 §33.5. Consequence, accent: A number, an outcome, or a detail only real experience knows.  
Purpose of this slide: Separate a demonstration of authority from an opinion (§33.5).  
Say:  
"Proof separates authority from a plausible-sounding opinion. It takes five to ten seconds: one specific piece of evidence, from real experience, that the point is true.  
A number, a real outcome, a detail only hands-on experience would know — any beats a general claim about experience.  
Keep it on the point just made."  
Cue: The greyed slice is the trap; leave it dark while you name it.

### SLIDE 07 — CTA (33.6)

\[2:42-3:07\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · CONTENT CREATION PRACTICALS · 07 / 12\. Claim, serif: Five seconds, one action, staying where they are.
