Status: nothing here is built. Section 8 puts visuals after the script is approved and after the Step A look gate. Day 1's five files, Days 2, 3 and 4's twelve and Day 5's Chapters 31, 33, 43, 44, 47 and 48 carry this same section in this same shape, against the same standard and the same vocabulary; this is that section written for a new chapter rather than a revision of an old one. It is written to CAMERA\_V2/VISUALS/SLIDE-ARCHITECTURE.md, the executive-density standard, so every slide is specified in the five layers with the component named from that standard's library, an evidence element with its provenance, and a consequence line the room can act on.  
The demonstration rule, applied to a chapter about what not to install. Every tool in a stack is invisible once it is installed, and its cost is invisible too, so the deck's instruments all put the tool and its cost on the same surface: a stack whose dark layers show which functions are covered without a new purchase, a gate whose failing exit is a partial tool, a cost ledger where the price is the smallest line item. No slide names a software product — the functions are named, the tools are not, which is the same rule the gear chapters applied to brands — so nothing on screen can be read as a recommendation.  
Build-stage sizes. One self-contained HTML file per chapter, 1920 × 1080 stage that scales, no internet, system fonts, three colours with the one accent, serif claim, sans elsewhere, no label under 32 px, lines at least 3 px, 8% safe margin, reduced-motion shows every layer in its final state. Build steps: 32 across the twelve slides, plus 1 for the supplementary board — 33 in total, and the deliverable index below sums to the same 33\.  
Slide 01 — The Software Stack Opens. Type: ten-layer stack, lit one section at a time. Build: 2 steps. Component: ladder / stack — the ten functions stacked as layers, each dark until the section that justifies it. Layers: chrome; claim, A stack should have a tool for every function it needs — and no tool for the ones it does not.; the ten layers; the dark-layers rule; the consequence line. What changes: the layers land, all dark; the second step lights the rule that a layer stays dark unless a tool is genuinely needed and brings up the consequence line. Why: the chapter's claim is that a stack's shape is decided by functions rather than by features, and a stack drawn with its layers dark is a budget before it is a list.  
Slide 02 — Recording. Type: existing-capture-against-added-application comparison. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger — the capture already in your phone or camera against a dedicated recording application, matched on what each handles: ordinary capture against screen recording and livestreaming. Layers: chrome; claim, Most stacks already own this function. Check before you add anything.; the two columns; the formats only one column covers; the consequence line. What changes: the columns land and appear interchangeable; the second step separates them on screen capture and live streaming; the third leaves the ordinary-capture rows on the existing tool and raises the add-only-for-formats rule. Why: recording is the function most likely to be duplicated by a subscription, and only a comparison can show a purchase that buys nothing new.  
Slide 03 — Editing. Type: three-level editor bench. Build: 2 steps. Component: decision bench — a simple mobile editor · a mid-range desktop editor · a full production suite, with how complex is your typical content? as the deciding row. Layers: chrome; claim, Choose the editor your content needs, not the one with the best reputation.; the three levels; the deciding row; the consequence line. What changes: the three levels land and the most capable appears the safe choice; the second step seats content complexity as the deciding row, which clears the suite for simple content, and brings up the upgrade-on-limitation rule. Why: the section's rule is that complexity of content decides, and a bench where the most capable option loses is the only way to show that happening.  
Slide 04 — Captions. Type: automated pass with a human review gate. Build: 3 steps. Component: gate / flow — raw footage through an automated captioning pass to a gate whose rule is has a human checked this against what was actually said?, with published captions and a misquotation, live as exits. Layers: chrome; claim, Captions are not an accessibility extra. Most of your audience watches muted.; the pass and the gate; the two exits; the consequence line. What changes: the automated pass fills and looks finished; the second step draws the review gate across it; the third routes an unchecked pass through the failing exit and raises the review-every-pass rule. Why: automation's failure mode is invisible — fluent, wrong, and published — so the only honest drawing is a gate that can refuse it.  
Slide 05 — Thumbnails. Type: purpose-built-tool-against-full-suite comparison. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger — a purpose-built design tool against full professional photo-editing software, matched on dimensions, text treatment and the speed of producing variants. Layers: chrome; claim, This is the image that decides whether any of the rest is watched.; the two columns; the variant-speed row; the consequence line. What changes: the suite column lands and looks like the serious choice; the second step fills the purpose-built column and the two separate on speed and fit; the third marks the concept-generation step as AI-assisted with the final choice held human. Why: the function is small and consequential at once, and matched rows show a small tool winning where the function does not need more.  
Slide 06 — Storage. Type: solo-against-team requirement comparison. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger — a solo operation against a team, matched on the section's three requirements: reliable syncing, capacity for real footage volume, access for everyone who contributes. Layers: chrome; claim, Storage is only solved when the person who needs the file can reach it.; the two columns; the access row; the consequence line. What changes: the columns land on capacity alone and look alike; the second step names the access row, which separates them; the third brings up the same-current-version rule. Why: storage feels like a capacity question until it is drawn as a person who cannot reach a file, and that is the row the section is really about.  
Slide 07 — Scheduling. Type: coverage gate with a partial-tool exit. Build: 3 steps. Component: gate / flow — prepared content arriving at a scheduling tool, with delivered on time to every platform you publish to and delivered to some, leaving the rest manual as exits. Layers: chrome; claim, Publishing should not depend on someone being free at the right moment.; the gate; the two exits; the consequence line. What changes: the tool lands and both exits light; the second step marks the platforms the tool does not cover; the third routes a partial tool through the second exit and raises the cover-or-publish-by-hand rule. Why: a partial scheduler is the costliest kind of almost-working tool, and only a gate with a partial exit shows work still left behind.  
Slide 08 — Analytics. Type: consolidated-view-against-native-dashboards bench. Build: 2 steps. Component: decision bench — a consolidated multi-platform view against each platform's own dashboard, with does this remove a recurring friction in how you actually measure? as the deciding row. Layers: chrome; claim, Measure less often, or you will not measure at all.; the two options; the deciding row; the consequence line. What changes: the two options land with the consolidated view in the lead; the second step seats the friction question as the deciding row, which keeps the free option alive for some businesses, and raises the make-measuring-happen rule. Why: the section's test is behavioural rather than technical, and a deciding row about whether measuring happens is the only honest rendering of it.  
Slide 09 — AI. Type: bottleneck wall with review marks. Build: 3 steps. Component: evidence wall — AI's places in the stack landing cell by cell: scripting and outlines · editing · captioning · thumbnail concepts, each carrying the bottleneck it addresses and a human-review mark. Layers: chrome; claim, AI is not one tool in this stack. It is a set of answers to bottlenecks.; the cells and their bottlenecks; the review marks; the consequence line. What changes: the cells land as capabilities; the second step attaches a named bottleneck to each; the third applies the review mark to every cell and raises the for-a-bottleneck-never-for-the-capability rule. Why: the section's discipline is that AI enters the stack as a solution rather than a category, and a wall whose cells each carry a bottleneck makes a capability-only purchase look unfinished.  
Slide 10 — Communication. Type: powerful-tool-against-used-tool comparison. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger — a powerful coordination tool against a simpler one everybody uses, matched on what each delivers: features available against work actually coordinated. Layers: chrome; claim, A tool half the team ignores coordinates nothing.; the two columns; the actual-use row; the consequence line. What changes: the powerful column fills with capability and reads as the better choice; the second step fills the simple column and the two separate on use; the third brings up the choose-what-the-team-will-use rule. Why: the section's requirement is use rather than sophistication, and use is invisible unless the two options are matched on delivery rather than on features.  
Slide 11 — Choosing the Smallest Useful Stack. Type: one tool's real cost, line by line. Build: 3 steps. Component: cost ledger — a single added tool with its costs beyond the price: time to learn it · time to keep fluent · another login · another place content fragments · another point of failure, totalled against the one function it serves. Layers: chrome; claim, Every tool costs more than its subscription.; the line items; the total against the function; the consequence line. What changes: the tool lands with its price alone; the second step adds the five costs and the ledger's total climbs; the third sets the total against the single function and raises the three-questions rule. Why: the chapter's last discipline is arithmetic its audience has never done, and a ledger that totals invisible costs is what turns it into a decision.  
Slide 12 — Close Of Chapter 50\. Type: the stack resolved at its smallest useful size. Build: 2 steps. Component: ladder / stack — the opening layers restacked with only the tools this business needs lit, one per function, and functions already covered left unlit rather than empty. Layers: chrome; claim, The smallest stack that performs every essential function is the right one.; the stack; the unlit covered layers; the consequence line. ## CHAPTER 51 — SOFTWARE WORKFLOWS

### SLIDE 01 — THE WORKFLOWS OPEN

\[0:00-1:10\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 01 / 09\. Claim, serif: A workflow is a route you can run the same way twice. Structure: a ladder / stack — the seven flows stacked from the simplest chain at the base, phone → edit → publish, up through the camera, conversation, long-form and transcript routes to the calendar layer, with backup and archive drawn underneath the whole stack as the ground every route stands on. Evidence: the chapter's own position — that every other workflow answers a specific limitation of the phone-native one, and should be added only once that limitation is a real bottleneck — sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51, opening. Consequence, accent: Match the route to the content, and run it the same way every time.  
Purpose of this slide: Pick up Chapter 50's hand-off and open the chapter as a set of routes rather than a hierarchy (intro).  
Say:  
"The last chapter chose the tools. This one is about the routes between them: the workflows that carry a source through to a published piece, and running the same route the same way twice.  
Seven flows follow, from the simplest possible chain — shoot, edit and publish on one phone — to the calendar that drives production and the backup discipline underneath every route, whatever kit you own.  
Each trades something for something: speed against control, control against time, time against reach. None is the advanced version of another. They are answers to different kinds of content, and most operations will run two or three of them side by side.  
And the rule is the one the gear and software chapters both arrived at. Add a workflow when a specific limitation has actually become a bottleneck — never because it looks like the more serious way to work."  
Cue: The flows are peers, not rungs; backup is the ground under all of them, so leave it lit from the first frame.

### SLIDE 02 — PHONE → EDIT → PUBLISH (51.1)

\[1:10-2:18\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 02 / 09\. Claim, serif: The simplest pipeline is not the beginner's version of the real one. Structure: a timeline with milestones — the whole chain inside one device: record · trim and arrange · caption and colour · export and publish, with no transfer, no conversion and no handoff between stages; the section's trade marked on the line as control. Evidence: the section's account of what a phone-native chain removes — a file stranded in transit, a compatibility mismatch, a wait on a desktop upload — and what it costs in colour grading, audio precision and preview size, sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51 §51.1. Consequence, accent: Use it for content where speed and volume matter more than polish.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the phone-native route and match it to the right content (51.1).  
Say:  
"The simplest pipeline available to anyone is also the one most beginners undervalue: shoot on the phone, edit on the phone, publish from the phone — no footage transfer, no format conversion, no separate editing station, no handoff between devices.  
For short-form vertical content especially, this is not a compromise version of real production. It is often the fastest route from idea to published post, and speed is frequently what decides whether a time-sensitive piece gets made at all.  
The trade is control. Phone editors offer a narrower range of grading tools, less precise audio mixing, and smaller preview screens that make fine visual judgement harder.  
So match it to content where speed and volume matter more than polish: daily clips, reactive commentary, behind-the-scenes material — any format where the audience expects rawness as part of the appeal rather than a flaw in it."  
Cue: The absent stages are the argument; say what is missing from the line, not just what is on it.

### SLIDE 03 — CAMERA → COMPUTER → EDIT → PUBLISH (51.2)

\[2:18-3:30\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 03 / 09\. Claim, serif: Every stage in this route is somewhere a workflow quietly breaks. Structure: a timeline with milestones — capture to card · transfer with an immediate backup · desktop edit · export · publish, with the backup marker fixed to the transfer stage and the time cost marked at each of the five. Evidence: the section's stage-by-stage account and its central constraint — added time at every stage, which is the deliberate cost of the added control — sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51 §51.2. Consequence, accent: Reserve this route for content where the quality difference decides the outcome.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the full-production route and name its five breakable stages (51.2).  
Say:  
"Where the phone-native route trades control for speed, this one makes the opposite trade. Footage is captured on a dedicated camera, transferred to a computer, edited in a desktop application, exported, then published.  
It is the traditional pipeline behind broadcast, corporate and higher-end work, and it stays right whenever image quality, audio precision or editing complexity exceeds what a phone can reasonably deliver.  
The stages are worth naming individually, because each is a place a workflow can quietly break. Capture writes to a card. Transfer moves the footage onto the computer — and should always include an immediate backup before anything else happens to the files.  
Editing brings the fuller toolset from the last chapter: multi-track timelines, precise grading, layered audio. Export renders the deliverable; publishing moves it to its destination. The cost is time at every stage, which is why it belongs where the quality difference decides the outcome."  
Cue: Five stages, five chances to lose footage or time; the backup marker is the one that must not be skipped.

### SLIDE 04 — ZOOM → RECORDING → EDIT → REPURPOSE (51.3)

\[3:30-4:42\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 04 / 09\. Claim, serif: Consent to record is not consent to publish. Structure: a gate / flow — a call being recorded with the other party's knowledge, then a gate asking has publishing permission been granted, separately and explicitly?, with clips extracted for publication and footage retained for internal use as exits. Evidence: the section's own requirement — recording enabled deliberately and with consent as both a terms-of-service and a courtesy matter, with the two permissions treated as separate grants made at separate moments — sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51 §51.3. Consequence, accent: Record by default, publish only with permission.  
Purpose of this slide: Open the conversation route on its consent rule, then teach the repurposing (51.3).  
Say:  
"A large share of usable content already exists inside conversations that were never intended as content: client calls, interviews, coaching sessions, team meetings, recorded presentations.  
This workflow treats a recorded call as raw footage — often high-value footage, because it captures genuine unscripted conversation that is very hard to manufacture on purpose.  
Before that: recording should be enabled with the other party's knowledge and consent, and consent to record is not consent to publish. They are separate permissions granted at separate moments, with publishing permission confirmed explicitly first.  
Then the file is imported like any other footage and reviewed for extraction: a clear insight, a strong quote, a useful explanation, a moment of real reaction. Each becomes a standalone clip, cleaned for pacing and background noise, captioned and published as its own piece. The discipline is recording calls by default, so a backlog accumulates from work that was happening anyway."  
Cue: The gate belongs on screen before the repurposing steps; land the two separate permissions.

### SLIDE 05 — LONG-FORM → SHORTS (51.4)

\[4:42-5:56\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 05 / 09\. Claim, serif: A lifted segment is not a short. It is thirty seconds of somebody else's context. Structure: a comparison ledger — extraction against re-editing, matched row for row: hook at the start, reframing to the platform's shape, pacing for a viewer with no context, a beginning of its own. Evidence: the section's own finding — that a segment lifted from the middle of a longer piece, with its framing, pacing and context unchanged, rarely performs as well as the same moment reworked for someone who has no idea what came before — sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51 §51.4. Consequence, accent: Cut each short as its own small edit.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the shorts route and the failure mode that hollows it out (51.4).  
Say:  
"This workflow repurposes content that was built as content: a long-form video — a podcast episode, a tutorial, a keynote — deliberately mined afterwards for shorter pieces.  
The relationship is not incidental. A long-form piece with strong shorts potential contains several self-contained moments of value, each able to stand alone without the surrounding context — and recognising that while filming makes this more productive.  
The process is a review pass for candidates: a strong hook line, a complete idea told in under a minute, a moment of real emotion, a clearly stated takeaway. Each is pulled, reframed for the platform, given its own hook at the start, captioned and published as self-contained.  
The commonest failure is treating this as extraction rather than re-editing. A thirty-second segment lifted from an hour-long conversation, with its original framing and pacing unchanged, rarely performs — the context that justified it is gone. Each short needs its own beginning, and often a tighter cut."  
Cue: The failing column is the slide; the tighter cut is the technique.

### SLIDE 06 — VIDEO → TRANSCRIPT → AI → CONTENT (51.5)

\[5:56-7:13\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 06 / 09\. Claim, serif: The video is only the first output. The transcript is the second. Structure: a timeline with milestones — record or select · transcribe · instruct the AI with a specific ask · drafted written pieces, with a human-review mark fixed to the final stage. Evidence: the section's sequence and its examples — summarise into a blog post, extract five standalone quotes, draft three follow-up topics implied by what was discussed — and its rule that the output is a draft requiring review, per Chapter 50, sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51 §51.5. Consequence, accent: Run every recording through it, so nothing sits unused.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the transcript route and why it belongs in a workflow chapter (51.5).  
Say:  
"This workflow treats a video's spoken content as a data source for work that has nothing to do with editing the video itself. The recording is transcribed, and the transcript becomes the raw material for an AI tool.  
The sequence runs: record or select the source video; transcribe it, with dedicated software or the feature in your editor; then feed the transcript to an AI tool with a specific instruction — summarise into a blog post, extract five quotes for captions, draft three follow-up topics.  
The output is a draft, and it gets the same human review the last chapter's AI guidance requires. It is not a finished piece on its own.  
It belongs in this chapter rather than a writing one because it only works now that transcription and AI drafting are cheap and fast enough to run every recording through as routine — one session becoming a written-content pipeline that used to need a separate person and a block of time."  
Cue: The review mark applies to the last stage; the point is the pipeline running every time, not occasionally.

### SLIDE 07 — CONTENT CALENDAR → PRODUCTION (51.6)

\[7:13-8:32\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 07 / 09\. Claim, serif: You cannot batch what you have not planned. Structure: an annotated chart, marked Illustrative — output across a run of weeks drawn twice: produced one piece at a time against the nearest deadline, which collapses in the week something goes wrong, against produced in batches against a calendar, which dips and recovers from a buffer. Evidence: the section's own argument — that a single busy week, a sick day or one equipment problem breaks the output of an operation producing piece by piece, while a calendar driving batched production builds in slack — with no measured figure available, so the chart is labelled Illustrative and sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51 §51.6 · Illustrative — not a measured figure. Consequence, accent: Batch against the calendar, not against the deadline.  
Purpose of this slide: Teach the calendar layer above the piece-level routes (51.6).  
Say:  
"Everything so far describes how one piece moves from source to publication. This workflow is the layer above: how a planned slate, organised on a calendar, drives production so content gets made consistently rather than reactively.  
The calendar holds the plan — what goes out, on what platform, on what date, and what stage of production it sits at. Production is then batched against it rather than performed piece by piece: several pieces filmed in one session, several edited in one sitting, several scheduled in one pass. Batching is only possible because the calendar exists — without a forward view of what needs making, there is nothing to batch against.  
The value is consistency under real conditions. An operation producing one piece at a time, driven by the nearest deadline, is fragile: one busy week, one sick day, one equipment problem breaks that period's output. A calendar driving batched production ahead of need builds slack, so a bad week draws down a buffer instead of halting."  
Cue: The chart is a shape, not a measurement; say the Illustrative label out loud when you point at it.

### SLIDE 08 — BACKUP AND ARCHIVE (51.7)

\[8:32-9:51\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 08 / 09\. Claim, serif: This is not a stage in the workflow. It runs underneath all of them. Structure: a comparison ledger — backup against archive, matched on what each protects and when: near-term loss against long-term loss, active files and recent footage against finished projects, a failed drive against a drive that fills up. Evidence: the section's account of both — a second copy of live work somewhere other than the original drive, and older finished projects moved off active storage on a regular schedule — and its rule that new footage is copied before a card is reformatted, sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51 §51.7. Consequence, accent: Copy first, reformat second, and never leave it until later.  
Purpose of this slide: Close the routes on the discipline that protects all of them (51.7).  
Say:  
"Every workflow here depends on footage and files surviving from capture to finished use — and that survival is not automatic. Backup and archive run underneath all of them; their absence is the commonest way a well-run operation loses work permanently.  
Backup protects against near-term loss: a copy of active projects and recent footage kept off the originals, so a failed drive, a lost phone or an accidental deletion does not destroy the only copy of unpublished work.  
Archive protects against long-term loss: finished projects moved off active storage onto longer-term storage, kept for their future repurposing value.  
The discipline is easy to state and easy to neglect: new footage is copied to a second location before the card is reformatted; active projects live somewhere automatically backed up; finished projects are archived on a schedule. It needs no expensive infrastructure — a second drive and a habit — but backup has to be a step in production. Later is exactly when the footage you needed is gone."  
Cue: Two columns, two different losses; land the rule with the card in it.

### SLIDE 09 — CLOSE OF CHAPTER 51

\[9:51-11:03\] · On screen: Chrome CAMERA · DAY 5 · SOFTWARE SYSTEM · 09 / 09\. Claim, serif: Pick the route the content needs, and run it the same way twice. Structure: the stack, resolved — the seven routes restacked with this business's own two or three lit, the rest left dark, and the backup layer drawn unbroken beneath all seven. Evidence: the chapter's own standard, that a workflow is added when a limitation has become a bottleneck rather than because it looks more serious, sourced Source: CAMERA Ch. 51, close. Consequence, accent: Next: the system that holds all of it together — the capstone.  
Purpose of this slide: Gather the seven routes, name the Day's last chapter, and hand to the capstone.  
Say:  
"That is the chapter: seven routes from source to published, each trading something for something, and none of them the advanced version of another.  
Shoot, edit and publish on the phone where speed is the point. Take the camera-and-computer route where control decides the outcome. Mine your recorded conversations and your long-form pieces for what is already inside them. Run every recording through transcription and drafting so nothing sits unused. Plan a slate and batch against it so a bad week does not stop you. And put backup underneath all of it.  
The discipline is choosing the route the content needs rather than the one that feels most professional, and then running it the same way twice — because a route you cannot repeat is not a workflow, it is a scramble.  
That leaves one chapter. Next: the system that holds all of it together, built for your business rather than described for anybody's."  
Cue: This close hands to the Day's last chapter and the programme's capstone — Chapter 56 — not to a break.

What changes: the stages land up to the AI draft; the second step attaches three named asks — a blog post, five quotes, three follow-up topics — to the instruction stage; the third fixes the review mark on the output and raises the run-every-recording rule. Why: the pipeline's value is routine rather than capability, and a mark that stays on the last stage is what keeps a routine from becoming an unsupervised one.  
Slide 07 — Content Calendar → Production. Type: two production rhythms across a bad week. Build: 3 steps. Component: annotated chart, marked Illustrative — output across a run of weeks drawn twice: produced one piece at a time against the nearest deadline, and produced in batches against a calendar, with the bad week annotated on both lines. Layers: chrome; claim, You cannot batch what you have not planned.; the two lines; the annotated bad week; the consequence line. What changes: the deadline-driven line lands and shows a collapse at one week; the second step draws the batched line beside it, dipping and recovering; the third brings up the batch-against-the-calendar rule. Why: the argument is about fragility rather than volume, and only two lines across the same week can show one uninterrupted and one broken — with the Illustrative label carried because the programme has no measured figure.  
Slide 08 — Backup and Archive. Type: near-term-against-long-term protection ledger. Build: 3 steps. Component: comparison ledger — backup against archive, matched on what each protects and when: a failed drive against a drive that fills, active files and recent footage against finished projects, days of exposure against years. Layers: chrome; claim, This is not a stage in the workflow. It runs underneath all of them.; the two columns; the copy-before-reformat row; the consequence line. What changes: the two columns land and read as one subject; the second step separates them on what and when they protect; the third pins the copy-before-reformat rule to the ledger's first row. Why: the section's whole risk is a confusion between two different failures, and matched rows are what separate a lost week from a lost archive.  
Slide 09 — Close Of Chapter 51\. Type: the stack resolved on two or three routes. Build: 2 steps. Component: ladder / stack — the seven routes restacked with this business's own two or three lit and the rest dark, and the backup layer drawn unbroken beneath all seven. Layers: chrome; claim, Pick the route the content needs, and run it the same way twice.; the stack; the lit routes and the unbroken ground; the consequence line. What changes: the stack lands as it opened; the second step lights only the routes this business runs and brings up the consequence line naming the capstone. Why: the close has to turn seven flows into a decision, and a stack lit on two or three routes over an unbroken base is that decision as a picture.  
Supplementary — the workflow-matching board (§51.1–§51.7). Type: content-type-against-route scorecard. Build: 1 step. Component: scorecard — the business's own recurring content types as rows against the seven routes as columns, with a mark for the route each type runs and a fixed backup column at the end that every row shares. Layers: chrome and the board itself, with the business writing in; no consequence rule, because the board is an instrument rather than a slide. What changes: the business names its content types, marks the route each one runs, and can see at a glance which types are being produced without a route at all. Why: the chapter's claim is that a route is matched to content rather than to preference, and a board whose backup column is shared by every row teaches the chapter's own shape.
